1:
The verse opens the disputed but treasured story of the woman taken in adultery, and the witnesses begin with the Mount of Olives. The grammatical-historical commentators fix the place and the reason: it lay about a mile east of Jerusalem (Barnes), and Jesus withdrew there, Gill says, “partly to decline the danger… in the night season,” partly to lodge with “his dear friends Lazarus, Martha, and Mary” nearby at Bethany (so Robertson too), “and chiefly for private prayer.” Lightfoot, uncertain whether he went to Bethany or “to some booth fixed in that mount,” recalls that the festival crowds pitched tents outside the walls within a sabbath day’s journey (Deuteronomy 16:7). Henry, for the Puritans, reads pathos into it: perhaps Jesus “had no friend there… courageous enough to give him a night’s lodging,” so that while his persecutors “had houses of their own to go to” (John 7:53), he must go “a mile or two out of town.”

The Latin fathers, through the Catena, find a mystery in the place. Augustine asks, “where ought Christ to teach, except on the mount of Olives — the mount of ointment, the mount of chrism?” For “the name Christ is from chrism… He has anointed us, for wrestling with the devil.” Alcuin develops it: the olive, “in the Greek signifying pity,” marks “the height of our Lord’s pity,” and as oil “floats above all other liquids,” so the Psalmist says, “Your mercy is over all Your works” (Psalm 145:9) — a fitting seat for the mercy he is about to show.

Ellicott raises, in passing, the question that hangs over the whole section: “the Mount of Olives is nowhere mentioned by St. John,” whose habit is to explain Palestinian places “for his Greek readers,” a small sign among many that this paragraph stands apart from the surrounding Gospel. The verse thus opens a narrative the church has long loved, even as the commentators begin to weigh whether John’s own pen set it here.

The verse belongs, too, with the close of the previous chapter, where “every man went unto his own house” (John 7:53) — Ellicott observing how “the artificial division into chapters often mars the sense.” The contrast is pointed: the rulers retire to their homes, the homeless Teacher to a hillside; and from that mount of prayer and pity he will come down in the morning to meet, with mercy, the very accusers his enemies are even now preparing.
2:
Daybreak brings Christ down from the mount and back into the temple court, where the people gather to him in a body and he takes his seat to teach them. Gill reads the return as evidence of character: it shows his “diligence, constancy, and assiduity, in his ministerial work, as well as his courage and intrepidity,” for he came back “fearless of his enemies, though careful to give them no advantage against him, before his time.” The courage and the caution are held together, not played against each other.

Robertson works through the wording clause by clause. The phrase for daybreak (orthros) stands in the genitive of time and is an old word this Gospel never uses, though it occurs at Luke 24:1 and Acts 5:21; John’s own word for the early hour is prōi, as at John 18:28, 20:1 and 21:4. The imperfect middle in “all the people came unto him” is pictorial, catching “the enthusiasm of the whole crowd now as opposed to the divisions in chapter 7.” The sitting down is an ingressive participle — he took his seat, Robertson adds, “as was customary for Jesus” — and the teaching an inchoative imperfect, so that the sentence shows the Teacher settling into his place and beginning. “So the picture,” he concludes.

The textual question surfaces in the same detail. Ellicott observes that the scene “agrees with His custom during the week preceding the Crucifixion,” comparing Luke 21:37–38, where Jesus teaches by day in the temple and lodges by night on the mount; but he records that the closing words, “and He sat down and taught them,” are missing from the Cambridge manuscript, “which is the oldest authority for the section.” Robertson frames the consequence as a plain alternative: if the paragraph is genuine, the day is the one following the last day of the feast; if it is not, “there is no way of telling the time of this apparently true incident.” The hesitation touches the dating, not the scene — a seated Teacher at first light, and a crowd undivided for once in its eagerness to hear him.
3:
Two questions run through the commentary on this verse: whether the paragraph belongs here at all, and what the accusers were about. Calvin states the first with his usual balance. “It is plain enough that this passage was unknown anciently to the Greek Churches, and some conjecture that it has been brought from some other place and inserted here. But as it has always been received by the Latin Churches, and is found in many old Greek manuscripts, and contains nothing unworthy of an Apostolic Spirit, there is no reason why we should refuse to apply it to our advantage.” Ellicott adds a smaller observation pointing the same way: “the scribes” are “never named by St. John,” whose standing term for the hierarchy is “the Jews.”

Clarke clears away the legend that grew around the woman. Some writers, he reports, gave her the name Susanna, married her to “an old decrepid man, named Manasseh,” and had her die a saint in Spain after following St. James — accounts which “the judicious Calmet properly terms fables.” What Clarke does accept is the historical setting: adultery had become so common “that they had ceased to put the law in force against it.” The waters of jealousy (Numbers 5:14) were no longer drunk, the suspected being too numerous; and there was a further deterrent, since “the men who were guilty themselves dared not try their suspected wives, as it was believed the waters would have no evil effect upon the wife, if the husband himself had been criminal.”

Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic record behind that collapse, noting first that Christ called the generation an adulterous one (Matthew 12:39; compare James 4:4) in a sense that “might be well enough understood in its literal and proper sense.” The tradition he cites is blunt: “From the time that murderers have multiplied amongst us, the beheading of the heifer hath ceased: and since the increase of adultery, the bitter waters have been out of use.” The Sanhedrin abrogated the trial by bitter water, grounding the repeal on the prophetic word “I will not visit your daughters when they shall go a whoring, nor your wives when they shall commit adultery.” The Gemarists name the author of that counsel as Rabban Jochanan ben Zaccai — who, Lightfoot observes, “lived at this very time, and was of the Sanhedrim; perhaps present amongst those that set this adulterous woman before Christ.” He thinks the scribes and Pharisees here were “no other than the fathers of the Sanhedrim.”

On their motive the commentators converge. Robertson calls the bringing of her “in itself an unlawful thing to do,” since “they had a court for the trial of such a case,” and reads the dramatic present tense and the placing of her where all could see as proof that the trial was staged for Jesus rather than for her — “they knew his proneness to forgive sinners.” Gill presses the hypocrisy: they acted “not because of their abhorrence… of the sin,” having by their own traditions all but voided the law, requiring a formal admonition before any penalty could fall. Men who had abandoned the ordeal because they were themselves implicated now invoke the statute they had let lapse, and arraign a prisoner outside the court appointed to try her.
4:
The charge is laid with every formality, and the deference is part of the formality. The grammatical-historical commentators note the show of courtesy: they address him as “Master,” which Gill judges to be done “in a handsome and respectful manner, the better to cover their ill design.” Robertson presses the legal language: “hath been taken” is the perfect kateilēptai, “caught and still guilty”; “in the very act” renders ep’ autophōrō, an old idiom (literally “caught in the act of theft,” extended to any crime) found nowhere else in the Greek Bible. The detail of the witnessed act, the commentators agree, is meant to make the case airtight and the law’s demand unanswerable — there can be no question of the facts, only of the sentence, which is exactly the ground on which they hope to snare him.

Ellicott records the variant of the Cambridge manuscript, the section’s oldest authority, which here reads “the priests say unto Him, tempting Him, that they might have to accuse Him” — naming the accusers as priests and bringing forward at once the statement of their motive that the Received text holds to v.6. Whichever the wording, the witnesses agree the verse exposes the accusers more than the accused: they parade a woman’s shame “in the midst,” feigning reverence for Christ and for the Law, while their real aim is to use her as bait. The very precision with which they state the case — caught, in adultery, in the act — betrays that their concern is not her sin but his answer, and that even her public humiliation is, to them, merely a means to an end.

The witnesses observe, too, the asymmetry the law itself condemned: Moses required the death of both the adulterer and the adulteress (Leviticus 20:10), yet only the woman is dragged before Christ, the man left unnamed and unpunished. Whatever the explanation, the omission underscores that the accusers’ zeal was selective and their aim ulterior. They had not come to purge Israel of adultery but to corner its Teacher; the woman, caught and shamed, was to them no more than the convenient occasion of the trap.
5:
The accusers state the penalty more exactly than the statute does, and the excess of precision repays attention. The grammatical-historical commentators observe that stoning was not the general punishment for adultery: the law simply commanded death (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22) without specifying the manner, and the rabbis took strangulation as the default where the mode was unnamed (Gill, Clarke, Barnes). Stoning was prescribed for a particular case — a betrothed virgin who proved false (Deuteronomy 22:23–24) — so Ellicott and Lightfoot infer the woman was either “an Israelitess… betrothed only,” or a married priest’s daughter, the Talmud distinguishing the penalties precisely (a betrothed daughter of Israel stoned, a married priest’s daughter stoned, a betrothed priest’s daughter burnt). Robertson agrees the case “may have strictly come” under the stoning rule.

But the legal nicety, all agree, is a pretext. The real force lies in “but what sayest thou?” — “a snare,” Ellicott says, “in which they hope to take Him whatever His answer,” like the question about the tribute money (Matthew 22:17). Gill marks that they cited “Moses,” feigning reverence for the very law their traditions had hollowed out. The dilemma they set is sharp: should Jesus uphold the death sentence, he would seem to usurp the power of life and death the Romans had withdrawn from the Jews, and to deny the mercy he preached; should he set it aside, he would appear to “teach contrary to Moses” and condone the sin. They suppose there is no third way — and so present a guilty woman as the instrument of their plot, careless of her shame so long as they snare her Judge.

The witnesses also weigh the broader irony of the appeal to Moses. The same men who in chapter 7 had been charged by Christ that “none of you keepeth the law” (John 7:19) now wield that law as a weapon, professing a reverence for it their own lives belied. By forcing the choice between Moses and mercy they thought to leave Jesus no escape; yet, the commentators note, they reckoned without the answer he was about to give, which would honour both the law’s holiness and the sinner’s hope.
6:
The question was a trap, and the answer to it was a silence. On the trap, the grammatical-historical commentators spell out the dilemma: if Jesus condemned her, Clarke explains, “they might have accused him to Pilate, as arrogating… the power of life and death, which the Romans had taken away from the Jews” (and Roman law did not even make adultery capital); if he acquitted her, “they might have represented him… as one who decided contrary to the law.” Barnes adds that they likely expected him to side against the law, as in the Sabbath disputes, and so discredit himself. Robertson notes the present participle “tempting” in its “evil sense,” and that “laying of traps for Jesus was a common practice of his enemies,” now grown into “a habit.” Gill locates the snare more exactly still. The accusers say nothing of the admonition their own traditions required before any penalty could fall — without which, he notes, a wife who confessed was punished only by the loss of her dowry — nor do they ask whether this woman should be judged by those traditions or by the statute. What they want is Christ’s own sense, “whether Moses’s law was to be attended to, or whether he would propose another rule to go by.”

On the writing itself the commentators confess uncertainty and offer competing readings. Lightfoot begins by setting aside the closing clause: the words rendered “as though he heard them not” he judges to have “of old crept into some books,” since Christ had already given proof enough that he took cognizance of the matter propounded to him, and yet stooped down and wrote a second time. Ellicott insists “any inquiry as to what He wrote is excluded by the fact that the narrative would certainly have recorded it had it been known”; the meaning lies “in the symbolism of the action.” Several manuscripts and fathers could not resist a guess — some copies add that he wrote “the sins of each one of them” (Clarke, Ellicott) — and Lightfoot ties the gesture to the trial of the suspected wife by the bitter water (Numbers 5), where dust from the temple floor was used. Calvin, for the Reformed, declines all such conjectures: by stooping Christ “intended to show that he despised them,” as one who “draws lines on the wall” to signal he is not attending; he expressly rejects even Augustine’s elegant idea that Christ wrote on earth, not stone (Exodus 31:18), to mark the difference of Law and Gospel. Wesley reads it more gently: “by this silent action he fixed their wandering, hurrying thoughts, in order to awaken their consciences,” and “signified that he was not then come to condemn but to save the world.”
7:
Christ breaks his silence only when they will not stop asking, and the sentence he returns turns on two words. The grammatical-historical commentators take “without sin” (anamartētos) not absolutely but “of the class of sins of which her sin was an instance” (Ellicott) — “the same kind of sin, adultery, fornication” (Clarke), as Barnes and Wesley agree. Of the immorality among the rulers that gave the word its sting, Ellicott notes, “evidence is not wanting.” The command that the sinless cast “the first stone” draws on the Mosaic rule that “the hands of the witnesses shall be first upon him” to put him to death (Deuteronomy 17:6–7); Barnes and Clarke describe the grim procedure — the witnesses casting the culprit down and hurling the first stone — so that, Calvin says, “greater caution might be used in bearing testimony.” Robertson pictures the moment: Jesus seemed embarrassed, but as much “because of the brazen hardness of the prosecutors as because of the shame of the deed,” then “lifted himself up” to give “an answer of which they think not.”

Calvin, for the Reformed, marks both the likeness and the difference between Christ’s words and the Law. The Law required the witnesses’ own hands “that greater caution might be used”; Christ presses the principle inward, so that this “very argument had weight with those slanderers, desperate as they were,” for “no sooner do they obtain a sight of it, than they lay aside those fierce passions.” Yet Christ does not, the witnesses insist, abolish the magistrate’s right to punish sin; he turns the accusers’ own consciences upon them, demanding that those who would execute the law be themselves clear of the very crime they prosecute. The single sentence thus disarms the trap without denying the law — and leaves every accuser to judge himself.

The witnesses underline that Christ’s reply neither acquits the crime nor accepts the accusers’ standing to prosecute it. He grants the law its force — let the stoning proceed — but fixes the first stone in a hand that must be clean of the same sin, and so exposes the prosecutors’ unfitness without ever pronouncing the woman innocent. It is, the commentators agree, a masterstroke that turns the trial inward: the men who came to judge are made to stand at the bar of their own consciences, and the law they invoked becomes the mirror of their guilt.
8:
A second time he bends to the ground, and the repetition is read as neither idleness nor confusion. The grammatical-historical commentators agree it was not embarrassment but design. Gill says that, “having said enough to confound them, and yet unwilling to pursue the matter any further, or publicly expose them,” Christ stooped again “that they might have an opportunity of withdrawing themselves without any further notice of his.” Ellicott reads it the same way: “the repeated action repeats His determination to avoid the office of judge. He has answered them, and He leaves His answer to do its work. There is a law written in their hearts, and this, while He now writes on the ground, is convicting them.” Robertson notes the variation in the Greek — the rare compound katakypsas for “stooped down,” and that “with his finger” is not in the best text — calling it simply “the second picture of Jesus writing on the ground.”

The same impulse to explain the writing that marked v.6 appears again: Ellicott records “a strange addition at the end of the verse, in one of the older MSS… ‘and wrote on the ground the sin of each one of them,’” a copyist’s attempt to give the action a definite sense. But the witnesses agree the point lies not in the unknown words but in the posture: by looking away, Christ spares the accusers his gaze and lets conscience do its work, so that they may retire of their own accord rather than be driven out. The mercy he is about to show the woman he shows first, in this small averting of his eyes, even toward the men who came to trap him.

The witnesses see in the double stooping a studied restraint. Christ might have answered word for word, exposing each accuser by name, but instead he writes again and waits, giving the convicted men room to leave with what dignity remained to them. This averting of his gaze is itself an act of the mercy that governs the whole scene — the same mercy that will spare the woman now first spares her accusers the public shaming he could have inflicted, and lets their own consciences, not his tongue, drive them out.
9:
Conscience does the work the law could not. One by one, the oldest leading, the accusers withdraw, until only Jesus is left with the woman still standing where they had placed her. The grammatical-historical commentators identify “they which heard it” as “the Scribes and Pharisees,” not the disciples or the crowd (Gill), and read the order of departure with care: “beginning at the eldest” means, Barnes and Clarke agree, “from those who were in highest reputation to the lowest in rank,” or, as Robertson and Dods put it, “from the elder men, as was natural, for they had more sins of this sort which they recalled” — “they are summoned to judge themselves rather than the woman.” Lightfoot calls the result “a thing little less than miracle”: Christ “had determined to shame these wicked men before the common people,” and his word carried “that peculiar force… that they could not stand it out,” but “with shame and confusion” confessed their guilt by retreating.

On the closing clause the commentators guard against a misreading. “Jesus was left alone” does not mean the temple emptied, but that the accusers were gone; the woman stood “in the midst” of the crowd that still surrounded the Teacher (Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott), as the discourse that immediately follows (v.12) shows. Ellicott notes that “being convicted by their own conscience” is probably a copyist’s explanatory addition, “the meaning quite clear without it.” The scene the witnesses paint is stark: the law’s self-appointed executioners, undone by their own consciences, slip away eldest first, leaving the sinner alone with the only One entitled to condemn her — who will not.

The witnesses draw the moral of the rout. The accusers came confident in the law and in the woman’s guilt, and left convicted by the one judge they could not silence — their own conscience. That the eldest withdrew first, Robertson and Dods note, is fitting, for age had only lengthened the tally of remembered sins; the very seniority that lent them authority lent them also the heavier burden of self-knowledge. So the trial they staged against Christ ends as a trial of themselves, and the crowd they meant to sway watches their silent confession of defeat.
10:
Gill fixes the gesture precisely: Christ raised himself from the earth over which he had stooped, and on which he had been writing. Robertson notes that the participle (anakupsas) is the same one used at v.7, so the verse closes a movement the narrative had opened — he had bent down, risen to speak, bent down again, and now rises a second time. In the interval, Robertson adds, “Jesus had kept on writing on the ground as the accusers had slipped away one by one,” and the result is that “no one dared to cast a stone at the woman on Christ’s terms.”

Ellicott presses for exactness in the question. “Hath no man condemned thee?” is more precisely Did no man condemn thee? — a plain past tense asking after a thing that did not happen; and the singular “man” is set deliberately against the plural “thine accusers.” The force is therefore “Of all who brought the charge against thee, was there not one to condemn thee?” Ellicott records too that the Cambridge manuscript carries a shorter reading at the first question, simply “Where are they?”

Barnes supplies the legal distinction on which the question turns. Christ had directed any innocent man among them to cast a stone, and so “to condemn her, or to use the power which he gave them to condemn her.” Not one had done it. “They had accused her,” Barnes writes, “but they had not proceeded to the act expressive of judicial condemnation.” Wesley glosses the question in the same register — “hath no judicial sentence been passed upon thee?” — and Robertson observes that the verb behind it (katakrinō), an old and common word for giving judgment down upon a person, is found nowhere else in this Gospel.

The point of the question, for Ellicott, lies past the law. Christ “has spoken words which have carried a lesson to them: he has now a lesson for her.” The enquiry is not a formality establishing that the prosecution has collapsed; it is “put to her to lead to thoughts of her sin.” She is made to say for herself that no accuser remains, and in saying it is brought to consider the charge that no withdrawal of theirs can answer.
11:
The climax — “She said, No man, Lord. And Jesus said unto her, Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more” — draws from the witnesses one united concern: to show that Christ’s mercy does not condone the sin. The grammatical-historical commentators stress that “condemn” here is judicial. Barnes: this is “the sense of passing sentence as a magistrate, for this is what they had arraigned her for”; Jesus “claimed no civil authority” and so “did not exercise it,” yet “regarded the action… as sin.” Robertson agrees Jesus “does not condone her sin” — compare “I judge no one” (v.15) — but “does give the poor woman another chance,” the command “sin no more” (the very words spoken to the healed man in John 5:14) meaning literally “henceforth no longer go on sinning.” Ellicott observes she offers “no plea for forgiveness… no attempt at defence,” and that though there is “no expression of forgiveness or peace as we find in other cases,” yet the words that bid her go “are the condemnation of her sin” even as they spare her person (John 3:17). Clarke records, with Bishop Pearce, how the fear that “I do not condemn thee” might “countenance… that crime” led the early church to omit the story from the public lectionaries — part of how it dropped from many manuscripts.

Calvin, for the Reformed, guards the point most vigorously. Christ did not “absolutely acquit the woman, but… allowed her to go at liberty,” doing nothing outside “his office,” for he “had been sent by the Father to gather” the lost (Matthew 10:6), and so “exhorts the woman to repentance, and comforts her by a promise of grace.” Those who infer “that adultery ought not to be punished with death” reason as falsely, he says, as if Christ’s refusal to divide an inheritance (Luke 12:13) abolished property law; rather “there will be no crime whatever exempted from the penalties of the law, if adultery be not punished.” Wesley sums the consensus: “neither do I take upon me to pass any such sentence; let this deliverance lead thee to repentance.”
12:
With the trap behind him, Christ turns back to the crowd with one of the sayings that define this Gospel. The grammatical-historical commentators recover the scene: at the feast of tabernacles, in the Court of the Women where Jesus stood (v.20), great golden candelabra were lit each night for the “Rejoicing of the Water-Drawing,” recalling “the pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night” (Ellicott, Robertson). Against that blaze of lamps Jesus makes “this supreme and exclusive claim” — he had called his followers “the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14), but that was light reflected from him, while he is himself “the true light” (John 1:9; cf. Psalm 27:1; Isaiah 60:19). Lightfoot and Clarke add that the rabbis themselves named “Light” a title of the Messiah and of God (“light dwelleth with him,” Daniel 2:22), so that Christ claims for himself what they ascribed to God alone.

The Latin and Eastern fathers read the claim against the foregoing scene and the chapter-7 dispute. Alcuin says that, “having absolved the woman from her sin, lest some should doubt… His power to forgive sins, He deigns to give further disclosure of His divine nature.” Bede notes he says not “the light of Angels, or of heaven, but the Light of the world” — of mankind who “sit in darkness, and in the shadow of death.” Chrysostom hears him answering the slur about Galilee (John 7:52): not a mere prophet of Galilee or Judea, but “the Lord of the whole earth.” Augustine turns it to exhortation: “let us follow Christ, the light of the world, that we may not be walking in darkness” — not the darkness “of the eyes, but that of the moral character.”

Calvin, for the Reformed, calls it “a beautiful commendation of Christ.” Since “we are all blind by nature, a remedy is offered, by which we may be… made partakers of the true light,” and the offer is universal, removing “the distinction, not only between Jews and Gentiles, but between the learned and ignorant.” Yet, he warns, men “will never present themselves to Christ to be illuminated” until they first own their blindness. Wesley adds the promise: he who “closely, humbly, steadily follows” shall have “the Divine light continually shining upon him… till he is guided by it to life everlasting.”
13:
The objection the Pharisees raise is not theological but procedural. The grammatical-historical commentators note the Jewish maxim that “no man can give witness for himself” (Robertson), and that the Law required two witnesses (Deuteronomy 17:6); since Jesus had only his own assertion, they held it “not true,” that is, “not pertinent,” “not worthy of belief” (Barnes). Ellicott catches the irony: standing “in the light of day, they demand a formal proof that the Sun has risen.” Lightfoot draws a vivid parallel from the rabbinic procedure for certifying the new moon — two known witnesses attesting before the Sanhedrin — which lights up Christ’s appeal to two witnesses, himself and the Father, in v.18. Robertson observes they were “still in the region of pedantic rules and external tests,” missing the substance for the form.

The fathers and the Reformers look past the technicality to the deeper claim. The Eastern Chrysostom says Christ “overthrew their argument”: “though I bear record of myself, yet my record is true” — an accommodation to those “who thought Him no more than a mere man” — and gives the reason, “for I know whence I come and whither I go,” that is, “I am God, from God, and the Son of God,” said obliquely after his “habit of mingling lofty and lowly words.” Alcuin answers their premise: far from witnessing alone, Christ “had, before His incarnation, sent many witnesses to prophesy of His Sacraments,” and asks why they reject “Mine and My Father’s testimony, the highest and most sure of all.” Calvin, for the Reformed, grants the common rule “that no man ought to be trusted when speaking in his own cause,” but the point is that Christ is no ordinary man pleading his own case. Wesley notes they “retort upon our Lord his own words” from John 5:31, to which he now replies that, being “inseparably united to the Father,” his case is unique.

The witnesses agree that the dispute exposes the Pharisees’ deepest error: pressing the letter of the law of evidence, they refuse the one testimony that could satisfy it, since the Father whom they demand as a second witness is the very God they claim to serve. They ask for two witnesses and will not hear either — neither the Son who speaks before them nor the Father who sent him.
14:
Christ does not dispute the rule of evidence; he denies that it governs his case, and the ground of the exception is knowledge. The grammatical-historical commentators stress the emphatic pronoun and the ground of the exception. Robertson: “even if” (kan) he bears witness of himself, “his own witness concerning himself is true… he can and does tell the truth all by himself concerning himself.” Ellicott explains why the canon fails here: “the requirement of two witnesses was based on the imperfection of individual knowledge, and the untrustworthiness of individual veracity,” but Christ’s evidence is “that of One who knew every circumstance” — “they claim a human proof of that which transcends human knowledge… a truth for which there could not possibly be a human witness.” Barnes adds that Jesus “knew by what authority he acted… by whom he was sent,” while they “could not determine this.”

The phrase “whence I came, and whither I go” the witnesses take as the whole compass of his person and mission. Clarke: “I came from God, and am going to God, and can neither do nor say any thing but what leads to and glorifies him.” Wesley sees in the two clauses “the two heads… to which all the doctrine concerning Christ may be referred” — the former treated in v.16, the latter from v.21 — and reads “whence I came” as “from God, both as God and as man.” The Pharisees’ blindness, all agree, lies just here: judging by the flesh, they cannot trace his origin or his end, and so cannot weigh the testimony of one whose witness rests on a self-knowledge they do not share. Their demand for a second witness is answered by the claim that the witness they doubt is the one being in the world able to speak the whole truth about himself.

The verse also reverses the charge. The Pharisees had said his witness was “not true”; Christ replies that it is precisely true because it rests on a knowledge no one else possesses. Where they see only a Galilean of known parentage, he sees, and speaks from, his eternal origin and destiny — so that the very self-knowledge they cannot share is the ground on which his solitary testimony stands unimpeachable.
15:
Two kinds of judging are set side by side, and the contrast rests on what each phrase is taken to mean. The grammatical-historical commentators explain “after the flesh” (kata sarka) as judging “according to appearance” and “carnal… prejudices” (Barnes, Gill): the Pharisees “looked at the form of human flesh, and declared His witness false” (Ellicott), judging by the standards of the flesh (2 Corinthians 5:16) rather than by the spiritual meaning of his words. Robertson sets it against the chapter’s theme: “the Light of the World had come, but they loved darkness rather than light” (John 3:19), blinded by “the god of this age” (2 Corinthians 4:4). Clarke hears Christ speaking “exactly in the character of an ambassador,” whose credentials, not a second voucher, prove his commission.

On “I judge no man” the commentators offer complementary senses. Barnes and Wesley take it of manner and time: Jesus “judged no one after their manner,” not coming “to censure and condemn men after the appearance” (John 3:17), and so “not thus, not now, not at my first coming” (Wesley). Calvin weighs the readings — whether the contrast is that they judge carnally while he does not, or that he refrains for now from the office of judge — and inclines to the point that they are “not lawful and competent judges, because they have not the Spirit for their guide,” while Christ’s judgment, when he gives it, is never “after the flesh.” The Latin Augustine, prefacing his homily, praises John as the eagle who “soared… above the whole army of angels” to the Word himself — a reminder that the One the Pharisees judge so superficially is the very Light their flesh-bound eyes cannot see. The verse turns their verdict back on them: the judges of the Light are themselves judged by the darkness in which they stand.

Gill notes a second possible rendering — “ye that are after the flesh judge,” that is, carnal men passing carnal verdicts on spiritual things — which only sharpens the contrast. The witnesses draw the lesson that judgment formed by appearances and prejudice can never reach the truth of Christ; the Pharisees, confident in their verdict, are in fact disqualified as judges by the very flesh-bound vision they trust, while the One they dismiss withholds, for now, the judgment that is his to give.
16:
Lest the disclaimer be heard as a surrender of the right to judge, Christ at once qualifies it. The grammatical-historical commentators dwell on the quality of the judgment. Robertson notes that the word is not merely “true” (alēthes) in the particular facts of v.14 but “true” (alēthinē) in the deeper sense of “genuine, soundly based… satisfying our perfect conception” (Westcott; compare John 1:9). Barnes is careful that the conditional implies no incapacity: in expressing his judgment of men or things Christ “was not limited, nor forbidden to do it, nor restrained by any fear that his judgment would be erroneous.” Gill grounds its reliability in omniscience: one who “looked into the heart” and to whom all things lie naked and open cannot be deceived.

The reason given is the Father’s concurrence. Barnes paraphrases it as a claim about coinciding verdicts. Christ concurs with the Father who sent him; the Father’s judgment his hearers would themselves allow to be right, and his own accords with it, since he was commissioned by the Father and would “coincide with all that God had purposed or revealed” — a commission attested, Barnes adds, by the evidence God gave in sending him into the world. Ellicott observes that although “judgment was not the object of His mission,” it was nonetheless “the result of the manifestation of the Light” (John 3:19), and is here identified “with the eternal and unchangeable truth of the Father.”

Calvin asks why Christ “does not rather make an open assertion of his Divinity,” and answers from the conditions of the incarnation: “as his Divinity was concealed under the veil of the flesh, he brings forward his Father, in whom it was more manifest,” so that everything he does and teaches rests on the Father’s authority. Wesley presses the union, and presses it both ways: “his Father is in him, and he is in the Father” (John 14:10), and therefore “the Father is no more alone without the Son, than the Son is without the Father.” They are not one God and another, he insists, but one God in distinct persons, and so inseparable. Wesley then meets the obvious objection — that the Son came from the Father to assume human nature and discharge his office on earth — with an analogy drawn from the way Scripture speaks of God himself: Christ “did not leave the Father, nor the Father leave him, any more than God leaves heaven when he is said to come down to the earth.” The judge who speaks is therefore never a solitary witness to his own verdict.
17:
Christ now meets the Pharisees on ground they had chosen for themselves. The grammatical-historical commentators note the pointed phrase “your law,” addressed “to those who were professed expounders of it and accused Him of being a transgressor of it” (Ellicott); Robertson observes the same idiom at John 10:34, and cautions that it does not mean Christ “separates himself wholly from the Jews and the law,” for he upholds it (Matthew 5:17). The rule invoked is the Mosaic requirement of two or three witnesses in a grave case (Deuteronomy 17:6; Deuteronomy 19:15; cf. Matthew 18:16), which Barnes presses to its conclusion: if two human witnesses establish a fact, “the evidence of Jesus and of God ought not to be deemed insufficient.”

Calvin, for the Reformed, anticipates the obvious objection — that no man is received as a witness in his own cause — and answers as before: “the Son of God ought to be excluded from the ordinary number of other men,” for “he neither is a private individual, nor transacts his own private business.” His distinguishing of himself from the Father, Calvin adds, is an accommodation “to the capacity of his hearers… because he was at that time a servant of the Father, from whom all his doctrine has proceeded.” Henry, for the Puritans, draws the devotional turn: “if we knew Christ better, we should know the Father better,” for “those who know not his glory and grace, know not the Father that sent him.” The argument thus stands: by the Jews’ own law two concurring witnesses settle a matter, and Christ offers two — himself and the Father.

Robertson adds a careful qualification: the combined witness of two “is not true just because they agree, unless true in fact separately” — the Law’s rule assumes each witness is independently honest, which is exactly the case here. Henry, looking ahead in the discourse, draws the believer’s comfort that runs beneath the controversy: “the time of our departure out of the world depends upon God,” so that “our enemies cannot hasten it… nor can our friends delay it,” and every true believer “can look up and say with pleasure, My times are in thy hand, and better there than in my own.” The two-witness argument thus does double duty, answering the Pharisees on their own terms while pointing past them to the Father whose testimony and timing govern all.
18:
Ellicott begins with the grammar: the Greek carries no word answering to the English “one,” so the clause runs more exactly “I am He who beareth witness.” Robertson, noting that the reading “the Father” is “clearly genuine here,” identifies the pair as the two witnesses Jesus presents to the Pharisees in defence of his claim to be the Light of the World at v.12. The demand for corroboration is met, then, not by producing a third party but by naming the Father alongside himself.

Barnes takes up the objection a lawyer would raise. Human courts bar a man from testifying on his own behalf, because he holds a personal interest in the case and the bench has no means of establishing that his evidence is impartial. With Christ the conditions differ. Where a man serves no party ends, is willing to deny himself, makes great sacrifices, and by his whole life gives every evidence of sincerity, Barnes allows that his own testimony “may be admitted in evidence of his motives and designs.” Such proof would still fail in a criminal trial, he grants, but the forum here is another: in an argument “on moral subjects, about the will and purpose of him who sent him, it would not be right to reject the testimony of one who gave so many proofs that he came from God.”

Ellicott unfolds the two strands. The first lies in Christ’s own individuality — “I, who know whence I came and whither I go, testify of Myself to you who know neither.” The second lies in the Father’s commission: he is “the Ambassador from the Father, accredited by the Father’s works and the voice from heaven,” so that his word is official as well as personal. Ellicott ties the argument to v.16 and asks that the whole be compared with the close of John 5 — as the judgment is not individual judgment because of the union with the Father, so neither is the witness merely individual.

What that second testimony consisted in, Barnes specifies: the voice from heaven at the baptism (Matthew 3:17), the miracles Christ wrought, and the prophecies of the Old Testament. From this he draws two remarks held deliberately together. A real distinction between Father and Son must stand, since both are represented as bearing testimony; yet “they are not divided. They are not different beings.” They attest the same thing, being “one in counsel, in plan, in essence, and in glory.” The Law’s requirement of two is satisfied, then, without any breach of the unity on which the entire defence rests.
19:
The question that comes back is a sneer, and it proves the very fault he had just named. The Latin and Eastern fathers read it so: Augustine says those who had heard “ye judge after the flesh” at once “showed that they did so,” understanding his Father “in a carnal sense” — “we see you alone; prove to us then that Your Father is with You.” Theophylact hears it spoken “in contumely and contempt,” insinuating either that he was “born of fornication, and knows not who His Father is,” or sneering at the “low situation of His father,” Joseph the obscure. The grammatical-historical commentators concur: Gill paraphrases the taunt — “it is Joseph the carpenter you mean; a goodly witness indeed!” — and Barnes notes it was asked “in derision,” the Jews professing ignorance of what Jesus had often meant by “my Father” (John 5:17).

Christ’s reply — “Ye neither know me, nor my Father: if ye had known me, ye should have known my Father also” — the witnesses take as both rebuke and revelation. He answers, Augustine notes, those who asked “to tempt Him, not to get at the truth.” The saying makes the knowledge of the Father wholly dependent on the knowledge of the Son: to know Christ is to know the Father, and to be ignorant of Christ is to be ignorant of God, however loudly one claims him. Calvin, for the Reformed, presses that the Jews’ boasted knowledge of God was empty, since “God is not known but in the face of Christ”; their question “Where is thy Father?” thus betrays a blindness not merely to Jesus’ parentage but to the God they professed to serve. Henry adds the comfort underneath the rebuke: those who would know God truly must “learn of Christ,” for apart from him they “become vain in their imaginations concerning God.”

Robertson and Clarke note that the Jews “professed ignorance” of what Jesus meant by “my Father,” though he had made it plain repeatedly; their question is thus less a request for information than a refusal of light. Ellicott observes that the saying gathers the chapter’s argument to a point: the Father is known only through the Son, so the demand to “see” the Father apart from Christ is self-defeating. The witnesses leave the verse on its solemn double edge — a rebuke to all who claim to know God while rejecting his Son, and a promise that whoever truly knows Christ has, in him, found the Father also.
20:
John closes the scene by fixing where it happened and why it ended as it did. The grammatical-historical commentators identify the treasury (gazophylakion) as the area in the Court of the Women where stood the thirteen trumpet-shaped chests for the worshippers’ offerings (Gill, Lightfoot, Clarke, Ellicott, Robertson) — “one of the most public places in the Temple area” (Ellicott), close by the very chamber where the Sanhedrin sat. Robertson notes Jesus “hardly taught within a treasure-chamber,” so the phrase means “at the treasury,” and reads the “and” as “and yet”: he taught openly, in the teacher’s chair, the very things that stung them, and yet “no man laid hands on him.”

The Eastern Chrysostom marvels at the Jews’ folly: having sought him before the feast, then found him “in the midst of them,” and often “attempted to take Him… without being able,” they “were not even so awed by His power, but set themselves to their wickedness, and desisted not.” He notes that Jesus spoke “in the character of teacher, which was more adapted to rouse them,” pressing the very claims of equality with the Father that enraged them. Barnes and Calvin draw the doctrine of providence. Barnes: the restraint “proves that God has power over wicked men to control them, and to make them accomplish his own purposes.” Calvin, for the Reformed, marvels that men who “held an undisputed sway” in the temple, and “might have banished Christ… by a single word,” were instead “constrained to endure Christ openly” — an “astonishing power of God,” who “caused men to hear him, and guarded him.” The clause “his hour was not yet come” (compare John 7:30), Augustine will insist, frees Christ from any “fatal necessity”: he dies not when his enemies will, but when he himself appoints.

Ellicott adds the telling detail that the chamber where the Sanhedrin held its sessions stood close by this very court, so that Christ taught “openly and fearlessly” within earshot of the council plotting his death. The witnesses thus read the verse as a quiet display of sovereignty: the One whose hour the Father alone appoints stands unguarded among armed enemies, and they cannot move a hand against him. The lesson, Calvin notes, is that no servant of God is in his enemies’ power a moment before God permits.
21:
Ellicott begins with the connective. The best manuscripts omit the name, reading “he said therefore again unto them,” and the “therefore” ties the discourse to what precedes — probably to the fact that no man had laid hands on him, his hour not yet come. He is still free to address the crowd, and after an interval does so. Ellicott pictures that interval: men gathered in small groups about the Temple, arguing over what he had said, some of them “really inquiring with earnest hearts.” He discerns “two currents of thought and feeling” in the court. One runs in “the honest hearts of the untutored multitude,” who “know little of argument, and dare not interpret the Scriptures for themselves, but in their rough-and-ready way… are grasping the truth.” The other runs in the priests and rulers, “a holy and learned caste” to whom the people are “in intellectual and moral bondage,” and who “seek to bind with their fetters hearts that are finding their way to the truth.” Some groups have moved off and others taken their place; seeing a new audience, Christ speaks again.

Henry marks the change of tone that follows. Christ “had piped to them in the offers of his grace, and they had not danced; now he mourns to them in the denunciations of his wrath,” though he still speaks “in kindness to those few who received his doctrine.”

The sentence falls in three parts. On the first, Ellicott prefers “I go away,” the same verb as at v.14, and fills in the pathos of the hour: it was the last day of the feast, and the thronging multitude would within a day be scattered “through all the extent of Palestine and the Dispersion.” He too is going away, and “many of them will never see Him again” — “there is in all the discourse the solemn feeling that these are the last words for many who hear Him.” The departure itself points, with John 7:33, to his death and return to the Father. On the second, Robertson calls the seeking “the search of despair,” a seeking of the Messiah “when it is too late, the tragedy of Judaism” (John 1:11). On the third, Ellicott objects that “in your sins” is “not quite exact, and is, perhaps, somewhat misleading”: the Greek is singular, and should be “in your sin,” pointing to “the state of sin, rather than actual transgressions” — the plural thought belongs to v.24, where the words recur. Barnes gives the force of the warning plainly: to die so is to “die unpardoned,” since “there is no way of pardon but by him” (Acts 4:12).

The fathers find in the going a freedom rather than a defeat. Augustine reads it of Christ’s passion “as a free, and not a compulsory sacrifice,” death being for him “a return to the place whence He had come.” Theophylact hears the promise that “He will rise again in glory, and sit at the right hand of God.” Origen presses the paradox that even his persecutors will seek him, though to seek Jesus is properly “to seek truth and wisdom,” and finds in the saying the proof that “He had power over His own death.” Calvin gathers the warning: the Gospel “is not thrown uselessly into the air, but must breathe” life or death (2 Corinthians 2:16); “the wicked will at length feel how great loss they have suffered by rejecting Christ… but it will be too late, for there will be no more room for repentance.”
22:
The question they put is mockery, and it is ignorant of what it mocks. The grammatical-historical commentators note the grammar of contempt: the form expects the answer “no,” Robertson says, but carries “a manifest sneer,” “alike subtle and bitter” (Vincent). They had earlier guessed, in scorn, that he meant to go to the Greek Dispersion (John 7:35); now, Clarke notes, “they understood that he spoke concerning his death,” and Ellicott explains their grim logic: “there is only one class of persons who can speak with certainty of thus going away — those who by their own act fix the limit of their own lives.” Robertson adds the cruelest edge: since the rabbis held that suicides went to the deepest Gehenna (so Josephus), the taunt suggests that “of course the rabbis could not join Jesus there.”

Gill marks the malice and folly together: the inference “by no means followed,” and in suggesting it they “imitated Satan,” hoping he might indeed do it and so “extricate them out of their difficulties.” Barnes weighs whether the question sprang “from ignorance or malice,” and reads in it “mingled hatred and contempt” — “he is a deceiver… he is mad, and it is probable he will go on and kill himself.” Yet, Barnes adds, the scene displays “the wonderful patience of Jesus in enduring the contradiction of sinners,” who “bore contempt without rendering railing for railing.” Calvin, for the Reformed, sees the same “fearless scorn” and “effrontery”: they reckoned Christ’s absence “a matter of no moment,” supposing they would “gain a victory over him.” The mockery, the witnesses agree, is darker than the mockers know: groping for an insult, they stumble near the truth — that his death will indeed be of his own laying down, and that whither he goes, unbelief can never come.

The chapter’s tragic irony deepens here. Twice now the Jews have wrenched a literal, contemptuous sense from words heavy with saving truth — first imagining a journey to the Greeks (John 7:35), now suicide — and each time their mockery brushes against a reality they cannot grasp: that he goes freely to a death they cannot share, and to a Father they do not know. Their scorn, the commentators agree, is itself the judgment Christ has just pronounced, the darkened mind of those who will “die in their sins.”
23:
The reply sets origin against origin, and nature against nature. The grammatical-historical commentators take “from beneath” and “of this world” as parallel terms for the earthly and corrupt: “you are of the earth,” Barnes says, “influenced by earthly, sensual, and corrupt passions,” while Christ’s “views are heavenly.” Robertson agrees the antithesis of katō and anō is “between the earthly (sensual) and the heavenly,” as in James 3:15–17 and Colossians 3:1 — “these proud rabbis had their origin in this world of darkness,” though he notes the language could glance at the saying that they came from Gehenna as “children of the devil” (v.44). Ellicott guards the sense: the gulf is “not that between souls in Abraham’s bosom and souls in Hades,” but “between heaven and earth,” the two pairs of clauses interpreting each other. Clarke reads it sharply against their taunt: “ye are capable of murder, and of self-murder too, because ye have nothing of God in you.”

Calvin, for the Reformed, finds in it the root of their unbelief. They “do not receive his doctrine, because they have an utter dislike of the kingdom of God”; under “of this world” he “includes all that men naturally possess,” pointing to “the disagreement which exists between his Gospel and the ingenuity… of the human mind,” for “the Gospel is heavenly wisdom, but our mind grovels on the earth.” Hence, he concludes, “no man will ever be qualified to become a disciple of Christ, till Christ has formed him by his Spirit,” and so “faith is so seldom found in the world.” Wesley simply notes that Christ here “directly shows whence he came, even from heaven, and whither he goes.” The verse thus diagnoses the Jews’ blindness as a matter not of intellect but of origin: earth-born minds cannot, of themselves, receive the wisdom of heaven.

The witnesses draw the pastoral warning. If the difference between Christ and his hearers is one of origin — heaven against earth — then no mere argument or evidence will bridge it; what is required is a new birth from above. The verse thus presses every reader to ask not merely whether he understands Christ’s words but whether he has been born of the Spirit who alone makes the heavenly wisdom welcome, lest, like the rabbis, he prove earth-bound in the presence of the Light himself.
24:
Two things in the repeated sentence draw comment: the change from the singular “sin” of v.21 to the plural “sins,” and the great claim folded into “I am he.” On the first, Ellicott observes that the singular pointed to “the believing not” as “itself a state of sin” (John 16:9), while the plural “brings home to them the definite and known acts of sin which resulted from their sinful state.” Calvin, for the Reformed, makes the same point: unbelief “is the source and cause of all evils,” not because it is the only sin, but “because it drives us away from Christ, and deprives us of his grace, from which we ought to expect deliverance from all our sins”; that the Jews “reject the medicine with obstinate malice… is their mortal disease.”

On “that I am he” the commentators hear the chapter’s deepest note. Robertson lists the possibilities — “that I am from above” (v.23), the Messiah, the Light of the World, the Deliverer from sin — but adds that the words may be taken “in the absolute sense as the Jews used the language of Jehovah,” the great “I AM” of Deuteronomy 32:39 and Isaiah 43:10. Wesley takes it so outright: “here our Lord claims the Divine name, I AM” (Exodus 3:14), as plainly as in v.58. Barnes keeps to “the Messiah,” the title Jesus had professed. Either way the witnesses agree that the verse fastens salvation to the person of Christ: to refuse to believe who he is, is to die unforgiven, for there is no pardon apart from him.

The witnesses also note the structure of the warning: the sentence is framed as a condition with one escape. The Jews are not told they must die in their sins, but that they will do so unless they believe — so that the very threat is an offer, the closing door still ajar. Christ presses the whole weight of salvation upon faith in who he is, leaving them, even in this stern word, the one path by which the sentence may yet be reversed.
25:
The question thrown back at him is contemptuous — “Thou, who art thou?” (Robertson, Ellicott), a phrase “in frequent use to express contempt” — and that they take his “I am” as an unfinished sentence rather than the divine Name, which by then was “too sacred to be uttered” (Ellicott). Barnes admires the patience with which Jesus, “a mere pretender from Galilee” in their eyes, “poor and without friends,” bore the scorn and “answered them.”

Christ’s reply — rendered in the Authorised Version “Even the same that I said unto you from the beginning” — is famously hard, and the witnesses divide over it. The grammatical-historical Lightfoot favours the temporal sense: “the same that I told you from the beginning,” pointing back to his open profession before the Sanhedrin in John 5. Clarke notes “a variety of renderings,” one taking tēn archēn as “the chief, the supreme” — “I am the Beginning” — and Robertson grants the sentence may be affirmation, question, or exclamation, while insisting the adverbial accusative “cannot mean ‘from the beginning’” in the simple sense. The Latin Augustine reads it doctrinally: “Believe Me to be the beginning” (the Greek archē being feminine), for “the beginning cannot be changed; it remains ever as it is.” Calvin, for the Reformed, rejects the rendering “I am the beginning” as a claim of eternal Divinity — “there is no ambiguity of this sort in the Greek” — and notes that even the Greek fathers “differ as to the meaning,” some giving tēn archēn the force of “altogether” or “this ought to be observed.” Wesley keeps to the plainest sense: “the same which I say to you, as it were in one discourse, with one even tenor from the time I first spake.” Beneath the textual tangle the witnesses find one clear point: Christ refers them back to all he has already claimed — Light of the world, sent of the Father — and bids them believe it.

The witnesses agree, beneath the grammatical tangle, that the question itself is telling. Having heard him claim to be the Light of the world, the bread from heaven, the one sent of the Father, they still ask “Who art thou?” — not from ignorance of what he had said, but from refusal to receive it. His answer, whatever its precise rendering, sends them back to his own consistent testimony; he will not frame a new claim for mockers, but holds them to the words they have already despised.
26:
Robertson reads the opening as a deliberate turn: instead of further talk about his own claims, already plain enough, Christ turns to speak and to judge concerning them and their attitude towards him. Ellicott agrees that the words arise from their scornful “Who art thou?” at v.25, and marks what follows as a withholding — there are present to his mind many things to say of them, and these, if said, “would be in words of condemnation; but He refrains.”

What the unspoken indictment would have contained, Clarke supplies in full: “I could speedily expose all your iniquities — your pride and ambition, your hypocrisy and irreligion, your hatred to the light, and your malice against the truth, together with the present obstinate unbelief of your hearts.” Gill grounds the restraint in omniscience rather than ignorance: Christ “knew their persons and actions… and all their sins,” and could justly have charged them with every one, “but this was not his present business, he came not to judge and condemn, but to save.” The reckoning is deferred, not cancelled; Clarke expects the charges to “appear in their true light” when, after the crucifixion, “the judgments of God shall descend upon and consume you.”

On the clause that follows, asserting the truthfulness of the Sender, Lightfoot offers a reading of unusual force: “he that sent me hath of old said and judged of you, and he is true” — the Father having long since passed sentence through the prophets (Isaiah 6:10; Isaiah 29:10), from which the warning “ye shall die in your sins” is drawn. Clarke takes it the same way, holding that whatever the Father has spoken of them by the prophets must surely come to pass, since his word cannot fail. Barnes keeps the plainer sense, that the Father’s declarations concerning men “are to be credited”; and Robertson draws the consequence that they “cannot evade responsibility for the message heard.”

Calvin opens the verse with an image of weariness. Perceiving himself “in the position of one who sings to the deaf,” Christ “pursues his discourse no farther, but only declares that God will defend that doctrine, which they despise, because he is the Author of it.” Calvin puts the thought in Christ’s own mouth: were he minded to accuse, their malice and wickedness would supply him with ample materials, but he leaves them for the present; the Father, who committed to him the office of a teacher, will not fail to fulfil his promise. He finds the same import in Paul’s “if we deny him, he remaineth faithful, he cannot deny himself” (2 Timothy 2:13), and draws from it a rule binding on every later preacher: by this example Christ “lays down a general law for the whole Church, that no man ought to be heard, unless he speak from the mouth of God.”

The closing clause Ellicott renders more exactly “I speak unto the world the things which I heard from Him” — truth “heard during the pre-incarnate life with the Father” and now announced on earth. He hears in it a studied contrast: the quiet of that origin, “the calm repose of the divine life in heaven,” set against “the misunderstandings and objections with which the manifestation of that life on earth had been encompassed.” From the men in front of him Christ turns to the thought of the One who sent him, and who is true.
27:
The commentators differ over how much the evangelist’s aside concedes. The grammatical-historical commentators weigh whether it was ignorance or unwillingness: Barnes thinks “they doubtless understood that he meant to speak of God, but they were unwilling to acknowledge that he really came from God,” while Robertson, with Westcott, blames their being “preoccupied… with thoughts of an earthly deliverer” and “prejudiced against recognizing Jesus as the one sent from God.” Ellicott finds the failure genuinely astonishing — “the statement of their want of perception… is made just because it was marvellous” — and pinpoints it: “they did not know that the Sender and the Father are one.” Gill ascribes it to a judicial hardening: “their hearts were made fat, and hardened, and their eyes were blinded.”

Calvin, for the Reformed, draws the sober application. “Hence we see how stupid those men are whose understandings are possessed by Satan”; nothing could be plainer than that “they were summoned to the judgment-seat of God,” yet “they are altogether blind.” This, he warns, “happens daily to other enemies of the Gospel,” and “such blindness ought to instruct us to walk with fear.” The witnesses thus read the verse as more than a note of fact: it is a window on the mystery of unbelief, in which men hear the plainest words about God and the Father and yet, for the hardness of their hearts, perceive nothing — a warning to every later hearer not to presume upon mere understanding without the softening grace of the Spirit.

The irony is one John intends. The evangelist, writing long after, records the failure precisely because it was so astonishing: men who prided themselves on knowing God could not perceive that the One speaking of his Sender was speaking of the Father, and of himself as one with him. The verse thus prepares the next, where Christ promises that only the lifting up of the Son of man will at last force upon them the recognition they now refuse.

Wesley adds that this very failure is why, in the verses that follow (vv.28–29), Christ “speaks plainly of the Father, and again claims the Divine name, I AM” — patiently meeting their dullness with a clearer disclosure. The witnesses thus see the verse not as the end of the dialogue but as its hinge: their blindness draws from Christ a still plainer word, so that the failure of perception becomes the occasion of a fuller revelation.
28:
The lifting up of which Christ speaks points first to the cross, and then past it. The grammatical-historical commentators note the word hypsoō, used in John of the crucifixion (John 3:14; John 12:32), and Ellicott adds that “both the Crucifixion and Ascension are implied,” the Jews now “marked out as the instruments of the Crucifixion” (Acts 3:15) and so the means of his return to the Father’s throne. Clarke notes that “to be lifted up” was a Jewish idiom “for to die.” The promised knowledge, Barnes says, would come “by the miracles that attended the death of Jesus… but chiefly by his resurrection from the dead”; yet Robertson warns it would be knowledge that “will come too late and will not bring a change of heart,” the Spirit convicting them “concerning judgment” (John 16:8).

The Latin Augustine hears in “that I am he” the divine Name: “Recollect the words, I am that I am” (Exodus 3:14), “and you will know why I say, I am.” The lifting up “means the lifting up of the cross,” “accomplished by the hands of those who should afterwards believe” — so that even his crucifiers might be saved. Calvin, for the Reformed, marks the severity: offended at their stupidity, Christ “declares that they do not deserve that he should open his mouth” further, yet foretells “the time will yet come, when you shall know that a Prophet of God has lived among you” — a knowledge that comes “too late,” when the reprobate are “dragged to punishment.” The verse joins Christ’s self-disclosure to his obedience: lifted up, he will be known as the great “I am,” who does “nothing of himself” but speaks only as the Father taught him.

The witnesses gather the verse’s two claims into one. The cross, which the Jews will raise in malice, becomes the throne from which the truth of Christ is proved; and the One there lifted up is shown to be both the eternal “I am” and the perfectly obedient Son, who originates nothing of himself but speaks only as the Father taught him. So the deepest assertion of his Deity and the fullest confession of his dependence stand together — the divine Name borne by the Son who does always the Father’s will.
29:
Against the desertion he has just foretold, Christ sets the one companionship that does not fail. The grammatical-historical commentators dwell on the unbroken fellowship: though “men had forsaken and rejected him, yet God attended him” (Barnes); Robertson notes that “however much the crowds and the disciples misunderstood or left Jesus, the Father always comforted and understood him” (cf. Matthew 14:23). Ellicott applies the words “to every moment of life,” a “Presence which they knew not of,” to which Christ would cling even in the hour when “the disciples shall be scattered… and He shall be left as men would think alone” (John 16:32). Clarke and Barnes ground the unbroken favour in Christ’s perfect obedience — “I delight to do thy will, O my God” (Psalm 40:8) — the Father’s “well pleased” (Matthew 3:17) resting on the Son who “always” pleases him.

Calvin, for the Reformed, widens the comfort to every faithful minister. Christ “boasts that God, under whose guidance… he does every thing, will assist him, so that he shall not labor in vain”; and “all faithful teachers ought to be endued with the same confidence,” knowing that “the hand of God will be near them” when “with a pure conscience they discharge such a ministry as he demands,” for God “makes his word successful by the secret efficacy of his Spirit.” The witnesses thus find in the verse both Christology and consolation: the Son is never alone because he never ceases to please the Father, and those who follow him in obedience share, in their measure, the same sustaining presence.

The verse answers the loneliness implied in their rejection. Surrounded by enemies and soon to be abandoned by his own, Christ is yet never solitary, for the Father’s presence rests upon his unbroken obedience. The ground of that presence — “I do always those things that please him” — is held out as the secret of all communion with God: the soul that delights to do God’s will is never left alone, but walks, as the Son did, in the company of the Father.
30:
A harvest in the middle of hostility is not what the narrative has prepared the reader for. The grammatical-historical commentators marvel at it as much as at the unbelief of v.27: Ellicott notes that “wonder has often been expressed at the want of apprehension” just recorded, and finds “no less room for wonder in the faith spoken of here.” Gill attributes the change to the manner and matter of Christ’s words — “spoken… with majesty and authority,” coming “with power” — and Barnes to “the convincing nature and force of the truths” he had set forth, by which “many… were made penitent and believing.” Both Barnes and Clarke quote the proverb that captures the double effect of the one discourse: “the same sun that hardens the clay softens the wax.”

The same word, the witnesses observe, had been “the savor of death unto death to the obstinate Pharisees” and “the savor of life unto life to many of the simple-hearted people” (Clarke; cf. 2 Corinthians 2:16). Yet the commentators note, looking ahead, that this faith would soon be tested: the very verses following (vv.31–32) address “those Jews which believed on him,” and the bitter dispute that ensues will show how shallow some of that believing was. For now, the verse stands as a quiet testimony that even in the hour of fiercest contradiction, Christ’s word was not spoken in vain, but drew a remnant out of the hardened crowd into the beginnings of faith.

The witnesses close the section on a note of hope tempered by realism. That “many believed” shows the word of Christ is never wholly without fruit, even where it provokes the fiercest hatred; the same truth that condemns the hardened saves the willing. Yet the commentators are careful not to overstate this faith, for the dialogue that follows will sift it severely, distinguishing a belief that abides in his word from one that withers under testing — a reminder that to begin to believe is not yet to be a disciple indeed.

Henry and the others find encouragement here for every preacher of the gospel: where the truth seems only to harden, it is at the same time secretly softening hearts unseen, and the labour that meets contradiction is never therefore fruitless. The verse stands as a quiet pledge that the word of Christ, faithfully spoken, will always gather its remnant, even out of a crowd bent on his death.
31:
Faith newly professed is at once put to a test, and the wording of the promise is exact. The grammatical-historical commentators note the precise phrasing: Robertson observes they “believed him” (dative autō, his claims) rather than “believed on him” (eis auton) as in v.30, so that they “did not commit themselves to him.” The condition “if ye abide in my word” (a constative aorist) makes “future loyalty… the test of the reality of their present profession.” Ellicott catches the note of wonder in the phrase “Jews and yet believers,” and links the “abiding” to John 15:7. Barnes presses the pastoral caution: their faith, born “under a single sermon,” had “had no time to test,” and only if it “should produce obedience… and a holy life” would it prove genuine, “for the tree is known by its fruit” (1 John 2:4). Henry, for the Puritans, hears Christ turning “from the proud Pharisees” to “those few feeble Jews that believed,” speaking comfort “to those that tremble at his word.”

The Eastern Chrysostom finds in “if ye continue” a searching of hearts: it “made it manifest what was in their hearts,” a “tacit rebuke to some who had believed and afterwards withdrawn.” He grounds endurance in deep-rooted doctrine, as the prophet prayed, “Nail my flesh by thy fear” (Psalm 119:120) — “the soul nailed by the fear of God none will be able to overturn.” Calvin, for the Reformed, draws the same lesson of perseverance: “it is not enough for any one to have begun well, if their progress to the end do not correspond,” and Christ “distinguishes his followers from hypocrites by this mark,” that “believers persevere constantly to the end.” The witnesses thus agree that this verse, addressed to fresh believers, lays down the abiding test of true discipleship — not the first stirring of faith but its perseverance in Christ’s word.

Augustine, for the Latin fathers, draws the humbling corollary: “we have all one Master, and are fellow disciples under Him,” for “He is the Master of all, who dwells in the hearts of all.” To continue in his word is thus not to graduate beyond the need of teaching but to remain, lifelong, a learner at his feet — the very posture the proud Pharisees would not take, and the test these new believers were about to fail.
32:
Both halves of the promise are unfolded, the knowing and the freeing. The grammatical-historical commentators take “the truth” as the gospel, and finally as Christ himself: Robertson notes that truth is “one of the marks of Christ” (John 1:14), who will claim to Thomas to be its personification (John 14:6), and that the knowledge is “learned by doing God’s will” (John 7:17). Gill spells out what the growing knowledge takes in: a larger grasp of the gospel, and of Christ himself — the dignity of his person, the nature and usefulness of his offices, the efficacy of his blood, the excellency of his righteousness and the fulness of his grace, and all of it, he insists, “for themselves.” That last qualification matters to him, since he sets these disciples against others ever learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth. Ellicott presses the same distinction from another side: these Jews “professed to know the truth… but they had yet to learn that truth was not only a system, but also a power; not only something to be written or spoken, but also something to be felt and lived.” Clarke calls it “a constant experimental knowledge of its power and efficacy.”

On the freedom the commentators agree it is deliverance from sin’s slavery, not from Rome. Barnes defines it as release “from the slavery of evil passions, corrupt propensities” (Romans 6:16), and Robertson links it to Paul’s great word for liberty (Galatians 5:1; Romans 8:2). Clarke sets the promise against a rabbinic maxim — that no man was free but he who exercised himself in the meditation of the law — and answers it directly: “no man is truly free, but he in whose heart the power of sin is destroyed,” who has received the Spirit of adoption and by it cries “Abba! Father!” (Romans 8:15). His summary is blunt: “the bondage of sin is the most grievous bondage; and freedom from its guilt and influence is the greatest liberty.”

Calvin dwells on the growth in knowledge promised to those who persevere. Though the men Christ addressed “were as yet uneducated, and scarcely knew the first elements,” he promises them “a more full understanding of his doctrine”; and because the statement is general, “whatever progress any of us have made in the Gospel, let him know that he needs new additions.” The deeper knowing is itself Christ’s gift, “for it is he who impresses his word on our hearts by his Spirit, and… daily chases away the clouds” of ignorance. Knowing and being freed are therefore one movement: the truth that liberates is not a doctrine merely grasped but a Person known.
33:
Two questions occupy the commentators here: who is speaking, and how the boast could be made at all. On the speakers they divide. Gill, Clarke and Wesley take them to be unbelieving Jews standing by, since the murderous words that follow (v.40, 44) seem impossible from believers; Ellicott and Robertson, with Calvin, hold rather that these are the very Jews who had just believed (v.31), whose faith, once tested, “fails in the first steps of discipleship.”

On the boast itself most of the witnesses are severe. Ellicott says it “passes the limits of historical truth.” Robertson calls “we be Abraham’s seed” the proudest boast of the Jews, but “were never in bondage” “a palpable untruth uttered in the heat of controversy,” since “at that very moment the Jews wore the Roman yoke,” as they had worn the yokes of Egypt, Babylon and Persia before it. Clarke judges the claim “ridiculous in the extreme,” their whole history being “full of recitals of their servitude.”

Lightfoot dissents, and his dissent is worth weighing. He first documents the pride of descent at length, citing the story of R. Jochanan ben Matthias, who told his son that though he should make feasts for his hired labourers “as gaudy as the feasts of Solomon, thou wouldst not do enough for them, because they are the children of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” — even while the rabbis conceded that “the merits of our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, ceased from the days of Hosea the prophet.” But Lightfoot then asks the obvious question — “Is it impossible that one of Abraham’s seed should be in bondage?” — and resolves the difficulty by separating the two clauses. The sense, he argues, is “We are of the seed of Abraham, who are very fond and tenacious of our liberty; and as far as concerns ourselves, we never were in bondage to any man.” On that reading the words are not a lie about national history but a claim about personal status, and he supports it from the law: the nation was “infinitely averse to all servitude,” and it was not lawful for an Israelite to sell himself into bondage “unless upon the extremest necessity.”

Calvin takes the charitable path by another route, reading the retort as a confused cry raised “by despisers rather than by those who believed,” and explaining the plural form by a habit of Scripture, which often ascribes “to all what belongs only to a part.” He observes too that they were leaning on their election and adoption (Romans 9:4), and could not bear to be told that a holy and chosen people lay under any bondage. On every reading but Lightfoot’s the answer condemns itself: taking an offer of spiritual freedom for a slur on their national liberty, they betray the very bondage of pride from which Christ came to free them.
34:
Christ answers the misunderstanding by raising the question from politics to the moral life. The grammatical-historical commentators stress that he “did not refer to political bondage, but to the slavery of the soul to evil passions and desires” (Barnes), the sinner being “bound to it as a slave is to his master” (Romans 6:16; 2 Peter 2:19). Clarke fixes the sense: this is “the slavery of which Christ spoke, and deliverance from it the liberty which he promised.” Ellicott presses the grammar — the present participle “committeth sin” expresses “the continuance of the deeds of sin,” not a single act — and notes that though the Cambridge manuscript omits “of sin,” the words “must be regarded as an integral part of the text.” Gill marks that Christ, “taking no notice of their civil liberty, to which he could easily have replied to their confusion,” instead presses home “their moral servitude and bondage.”

Calvin, for the Reformed, draws the doctrine of the will’s bondage: the man who serves sin is no free agent but a slave, however he boasts of liberty, and only Christ can break the chain. Wesley adds that the bondage is universal until grace intervenes, and Cyril of Jerusalem turns the saying toward the deliverance of baptismal grace. The witnesses thus see the verse exposing the deepest irony of the Jews’ boast: priding themselves that they “were never in bondage,” they were, every one, the slaves of the sin that ruled them — and the freedom Christ offered was precisely the freedom from this servitude that no descent from Abraham could supply. The Son alone, the next verses will say, can make a slave a free son of the house.
