The witnesses press the universality of the diagnosis. “Whosoever” admits no exception: Jew and Gentile, free citizen and slave, the man who keeps on sinning is sin’s bondsman, whatever his birth or station. This levels every proud distinction the Jews had raised, and prepares the gospel offer — that since all alike are slaves, all alike need the one Liberator, and the only freedom worth the name is the freedom from sin that the Son bestows.
35:
The household metaphor is pressed a step further, from the standing of a slave to the standing of a son. The grammatical-historical commentators hear an allusion to Abraham’s own household: the slave Hagar and her son Ishmael were cast out, while Isaac, the son, remained the heir (Gill, Barnes, Ellicott; cf. Genesis 21:10; Galatians 4:30). The point, they explain, is that a slave “has no permanent standing in the family”; his place is precarious and may be ended at any time, whereas “the Son abideth ever.” So the Jews, slaves of sin, have no abiding place in God’s house by mere natural descent; only sonship secures a permanent inheritance. Robertson and Ellicott note the deliberate ambiguity of “the Son” — the figure of any true son in a household, but pointing beyond to the Son who abides eternally and alone can confer the freedom of sons.

Calvin, for the Reformed, draws the warning and the comfort together. The bondservant’s insecure tenure is the lot of all who remain in sin; they may dwell for a time in the visible church, as Ishmael in Abraham’s tent, but “shall not abide for ever.” Yet the Son’s eternal abiding is the ground of the believer’s hope, for those whom he makes free and adopts share his permanence in the Father’s house. The witnesses thus find in the verse a quiet but searching threat to the presumptuous — that physical kinship with Abraham, like a slave’s place in the house, gives no lasting title — and the promise that only union with the abiding Son makes one a son who abides.

The witnesses add that the figure quietly answers the Jews’ confidence in mere membership of the covenant people. To be in the house as a servant is not to belong to it as a son; and a servant may be put out, as Ishmael was. So the warning falls on all who rest in outward privilege — natural descent, ritual standing, a place in the visible church — without the sonship that the abiding Son alone confers. Privilege without faith, the verse implies, is a tenancy that can be ended.
36:
The conclusion Christ draws turns on a single adverb. The grammatical-historical commentators note that the word behind “indeed” (ontōs) is not the one rendered “indeed” a few lines earlier at v.31; it means “actually, really,” and Ellicott accordingly renders the promise “ye shall be free in reality.” Robertson parses the sentence as a condition of the third class with an ingressive aorist — “if therefore the Son set you free,” as he has the power to do — and observes that such liberty “was beyond the concept or wish of these Jews.” Barnes grounds the power in the person: the Son of God, “heir of all things,” is “for ever with God, and who has therefore the right and power to liberate men from their thraldom,” and the deliverance he gives is “not from the chains and oppressions of earthly masters and monarchs, but from the bondage of sin.”

Ellicott sets the word “reality” against three boasts in turn. They claimed political freedom, “but they were in reality the subjects of Rome”; religious freedom, but “in reality the slaves to the letter”; moral freedom, but “in reality the bondmen of sin.” Over against all three stands a liberty no power can restrain, and Ellicott finds its fullest illustration in Paul, who called himself a bondservant yet stood before Agrippa and lay a prisoner at Rome more truly free than the governor or the Caesar who judged him: “the chains that bind the body cannot bind the spirit, whose chains have been loosed.”

Gill hears behind the promise a usage of the ancient household. The Greeks knew a form of adoption by the sons or brethren of a family — “the adoption of brethren,” as Grotius and others observed — and the Romans a custom whereby a son, after his father’s death, might emancipate those born slaves in the house. The freed bondsman does not merely change masters; he is taken into the family. Calvin presses the same point doctrinally: the right of freedom “belongs to himself alone,” and what the Son “possesses as his own by nature he imparts to us by adoption, when we are ingrafted by faith into his body, and become his members.” Freedom is thus a benefit conferred by Christ and received by faith, and Calvin supplies the contrast the Jews had invited — their “foolish persuasion,” the pride by which, “in like manner as the greater part of the world,” men “imagine that they possess a kingdom, while they are in the most wretched bondage.” Wesley reads the verse as the promise of a share in that liberty, real and entire.
37:
Christ grants the descent and denies the kinship, and the commentators mark both the concession and its limit. He “admits that you are the descendants of Abraham” (Barnes), yet shows that “they might be his descendants and still lack entirely his spirit” (compare Matthew 3:9). Gill states the principle behind the concession plainly — “truth must be allowed to an adversary” — and then shows how little it secures: natural descent left them still “in moral bondage to sin,” and a man may be cast out of the house of God “as Ishmael was cast out of Abraham’s, though he was his natural seed.” Ellicott observes that Christ takes up their own word, “seed,” acknowledging “merely physical descent,” while refusing “to acknowledge that they are Abraham’s children” (v.39).

The proof of the denial is their murderous intent (John 7:30) and the failure of his word to find lodging. Robertson glosses the verb (chōrei), “to have space or room for,” as “hath not free course”: “they had no longer room for his word when once they understood the spiritual aspect of his message,” so that “Jerusalem was now just like Galilee once before” (John 6:60–66). Clarke takes the same figure further, and turns it on the hearer. The word, on his reading, “requires a heart which is empty”; and a heart “filled with earthly projects, carnal interests, ambition, thoughts of raising a fortune, and with the love of the superfluities and pleasures of life, is not fit to receive the seed of the kingdom.” He sets out a progression of guilt, borrowed from Quesnel: “it is a dismal omen when a person is regardless of the truth of God: it is more so to be provoked against it: but to persecute and endeavor to destroy those who preach it is the last degree of perverseness and obduracy.” And the closing of the heart is never merely negative — “when a man shuts his heart against it by his passions, he at the same time opens it to all sorts of crimes.”

The fathers and Reformers press the gravity of a word that finds no room. Chrysostom says Christ “reminds them of a present sin… actually at this moment in their thoughts,” loosening them “by degrees out of their relationship to Abraham.” Henry, for the Puritans, likens them to “a sick person who turns from his physician, and will take neither remedies nor food,” who is “past hope of recovery,” for “where the word of God has no place, no good is to be expected.” Calvin reads the concession as ridicule of their pride: granting the title they prize, “what avails it that those men are called Abraham’s seed, who are enraged against God and his ministers… and rush headlong to shed innocent blood?” Lightfoot hears the whole drift of the discourse pointing toward v.44, where they will be named the seed of the serpent that was to bruise the heel of the Messiah.
38:
The difference between speaker and hearers is traced to two origins, and the commentators dwell on the two fathers. Robertson reads “with my Father” (para tō patri, locative) as “by the side of my Father,” a “picture of intimate fellowship” like the “face to face with God” of John 1:1, and insists that although the same construction serves for “your father,” the noun “does not mean the same person — Christ’s Father by contrast is not their father.” Ellicott marks the “direct opposition” of the emphatic pronouns: “I, on My part… My Father. You, on your part… your father.” He connects the verse with v.28, where the same link between doing and speaking appears, and puts the matter christologically: “He is the Word, and His work is to speak what He had seen in His eternal existence with the Father.”

Several of the commentators prefer a different reading in the second clause — “ye do that which ye have heard with your father” — since, as Clarke observes with Bishop Pearce, “it could not be said… that the Jews had seen any thing with their father the devil, as it could that Jesus had seen with his.” Ellicott, who also prefers “heard,” shows how much turns on the change. The tenses are to be distinguished: “that which I have seen” covers Christ’s “whole existence in eternity,” while “that which ye heard” dates from the moment “ye became servants of sin.” So do the cases: Christ “saw with” his Father, which signifies existence alongside him, whereas they “heard from” theirs, which signifies receiving his directions. Ellicott notes besides a word in the Greek that the English version drops altogether: the sense is not simply “and ye do,” but “and ye therefore, or accordingly, do.” The parallel is therefore exact and damning — “it is the same principle of union between Father and Son which directs His work, which is to reveal God, and their work, of which the seeking to kill Him is an instance.” He records too that some manuscripts read “the” for “My,” and some omit the possessive with “father,” without change of sense.

Henry makes the verse the watershed of the chapter: “here are two fathers spoken of, according to the two families into which the sons of men are divided — God and the devil — and without controversy these are contrary the one to the other.” Christ’s doctrine, he says, “was copied out of the counsels of infinite wisdom,” while their deeds were learned in another school. Calvin reads it as an argument “drawn from contrary things”: since Christ brings only what he has learned from his Father, their fury against his word proves they have an opposite father; and by that reasoning he “protects the Gospel against contempt,” since it is no wonder if such men oppose it. The line drawn here is not one of blood but of the father whose directions a man carries out — and v.44 will name him.
39:
The retreat is to genealogy, and the answer draws a line between seed and children. Feeling the unspoken charge (v.44), they “claim the descent from Abraham which He has already allowed” (Ellicott). Christ replies by a principle Barnes states generally: “the words sons and children are often used to denote those who imitate another or who have his spirit” — so that “if you were worthy to be called the children of Abraham, or if you had his spirit,” you would do his works, imitating him, as Clarke puts it, “in his faith, obedience, and uprightness.” Ellicott sharpens the distinction: “they are the physical seed of the patriarch, but they are not the ethical children, for the true child would bear the moral impress of the father.” Robertson notes the text-critical tangle — the better reading gives “if ye are,” a condition of the first class, against the “ye would do” that follows — but the force is not in doubt: their deeds belie their claim.

Calvin reads the exchange as a case study in how a title can blind a man. What they vaunt is not merely lineal descent but that they are “a holy race, the heritage of God, and the children of God”; and yet “they rely on nothing but the confidence of the flesh.” His verdict is flat: “carnal descent, without faith, is nothing more than a false pretense.” This, he thinks, explains how men could treat with disdain a word “which might move stones” — and he turns it at once upon his own age, where the same word is ridiculed and persecuted by those who “rely on their false title of ‘the Church.’” The mechanism is general: “as soon as hypocrites have procured some plausible covering, they oppose God with hardened obstinacy, as if he could not penetrate into their hearts.”

Calvin then grounds the distinction in the covenant rather than in character alone. He is careful that the argument is not about carnal descent as such, but about whether those “who do not retain by faith the grace of adoption” are reckoned Abraham’s children before God. The promise ran, “I will establish my covenant between me and thee, and thy seed after thee, in their generations, for an everlasting covenant, to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee” (Genesis 17:7); and unbelievers, “by rejecting this promise,” excluded themselves. So he states the question precisely: ought men to be accounted Abraham’s children who reject the blessing offered them in the word, and yet remain “a holy nation, the heritage of God, and a royal priesthood” (Exodus 19:6)? He denies it, “and justly; for they who are the children of the promise must be born again by the Spirit,” and all who would have a place in the kingdom “ought to be new creatures.” Yet he refuses to make descent worthless: it “was not indeed useless, and of no value, provided that the truth were added to it. For election dwells in the seed of Abraham, but it is free,” so that those “whom God sanctifies by his Spirit are accounted heirs of life.”
40:
The argument of the preceding verse is clinched by a deed. A true child of Abraham would imitate Abraham; these men seek to kill one who has told them the truth he heard from God — and “this did not Abraham.” Robertson calls the closing sentence “blunt and pointed of their unlikeness to Abraham,” and notes that the “but now” marks a plain statement that they are not doing the works of Abraham at all. Ellicott puts the same thing as a contrast of fact against character: “in opposition to the conduct which would characterise the true children of Abraham, ye are seeking to kill Me.”

Both men dwell on the word “a man.” Robertson explains the grammar: the noun stands in apposition to the pronoun, and the verb that follows is first person singular because the relative takes the person of “me” — “an idiom not retained in the English,” though English keeps it at 1 Corinthians 15:9 with “that am.” He adds that “God” here is equivalent to “My Father” in v.38, and sums the matter up: “the only crime of Jesus is telling the truth directly from God.” Ellicott reads the term theologically: “a man” “expresses His revelation, by means of human form, of the divine truth which He heard in the pre-human state,” so that the crime is doubly aggravated — “they seek to destroy the human life which for the sake of humanity He has assumed.” Cyril of Jerusalem presses the same word against a later error: “a man who has told you the truth” silences those who “speak against His humanity,” since Christ owns himself truly man in the very act of bringing the truth of God.

On the closing clause Ellicott parts company with the common reading. “It is usual,” he grants, “to explain these words by a reference to Abraham’s receptivity of the divine truth and messengers” — the welcome given at Mamre and the obedience of the later chapters of his life (Genesis 12; 18; 22). But he thinks the words reach wider, and “probably point to the whole course of the patriarchal life as directly opposed to the spirit of those who claim to be his children.” The contrast is not with one episode of hospitality but with a whole manner of living.

Calvin marks the heinousness the verse exposes. They are “not merely murderers,” but men “driven to such rage by hatred of God and his truth,” which he judges “far more heinous.” So the works, and not the blood, declare the father; and a people bent on killing the truthful messenger of God have answered the question of descent themselves, in the terms the next verses will make explicit.
41:
The unnamed father is now plainly in view, and the Jews answer by leaping from Abraham to God. The grammatical-historical commentators observe Christ’s restraint: he “repeats the charge… as if unwilling to name Satan as their father,” choosing that “they should infer whom he meant” (Barnes). They, sensing “a spiritual father is intended” (Ellicott), abandon the appeal to Abraham and “claim God as their Father.” Their retort “We be not born of fornication” the commentators read against the prophetic use of fornication for idolatry (Isaiah 1:21; Jeremiah): they protest they are no idolatrous, spurious race but worship the one true God (Clarke, Ellicott). Robertson notes the proud boast, and the “vaguely possible” bitter edge — “an indirect fling at Jesus as the bastard son of Mary” — which Origen too detects, hearing them “insinuate that our Saviour was the offspring of adultery.”

Calvin, for the Reformed, exposes the false syllogism beneath their confidence: “God adopted for himself the family of Abraham; therefore, since we are Abraham’s descendants, we must be the children of God.” They “imagined that God was bound to the whole seed of Abraham,” supposing “they had holiness from the womb, because they were sprung from a holy root” — the very error, he adds, of “the Papists in the present day,” who vaunt their succession. The Latin Augustine and Cyril of Jerusalem press the principle that decides the matter: spiritual sonship is by imitation, not birth. As Paul became “the father of the Corinthians” by his teaching, so “the devil is called the father of those who of their own will consent unto him” (Cyril). The witnesses thus find the Jews’ boast — God their only Father — already refuted by the deeds that betray another paternity, which Christ is about to name outright.

The witnesses observe how the dialogue tightens like a net. Each claim the Jews advance — Abraham’s seed, then God their Father — Christ allows only to overturn it by their works, so that their genealogy and their religion alike become witnesses against them. The very vehemence with which they deny a lowly birth betrays how much they trusted in birth itself; and that trust, Calvin notes, is the root error from which their whole resistance to the gospel grows.
42:
The claim to have God for Father is answered by a test, and the test is love. The grammatical-historical commentators draw the logic out: God’s true children “would bear the spiritual image of their Father, and would love Him who came from God” (Ellicott), but they were seeking to kill him (v.40). Barnes makes it a chain: “all who truly love God, love his Son Jesus Christ,” for “every one that loveth him that begat, loveth him also that is begotten of him” (1 John 5:1); so those who “reject his Son… have no evidence that they are the friends of God.” Robertson notes the second-class condition “ye would love me,” which carries “the distinct implication that their failure to love Jesus is proof that God is not their Father,” and hears in “I proceeded forth from God” (exēlthon ek tou theou) “the definite consciousness of pre-existence with God” (John 17:5), the Incarnation being “the mission of the Son who proceeded from the Father” (Ellicott; cf. John 16:27).

Calvin, for the Reformed, frames the argument tightly: “whoever is a child of God will acknowledge his first-born Son; but you hate me, and therefore you have no reason to boast that you are God’s children.” He draws the abiding principle: “there is no piety and no fear of God where Christ is rejected,” and “how can they agree with the Father who disagree with his only Son?” Hypocritical religion may shelter “under the name of God,” but a knowledge of God “in which his lively image is rejected” is no knowledge at all. Wesley adds the compact note that Christ “proceeded forth as God, and came as Christ.” The witnesses thus make love of Christ the infallible mark of true sonship to God: to claim the Father while hating the Son is to refute oneself.

The witnesses press the searching application. If love of Christ is the test of true sonship to God, then no profession of religion, however zealous, can stand where that love is absent. The Jews’ hatred of Jesus is thus not a side-issue but the disproof of their deepest claim; and the same test, the commentators note, falls on every age — that those who reject the Son, whatever their reverence for God’s name, show thereby that they are not his children.
43:
Two words for speaking stand in the question, and the commentators keep them apart. The grammatical-historical commentators preserve the distinction between “speech” (lalia, the manner or form of words) and “word” (logos, the matter spoken): Ellicott and Robertson agree that they “will not listen to the substance of Christ’s teaching, and hence they are impatient with the way that he talks.” The key is the sense of “cannot hear.” Barnes explains that “hear” here means “bear or tolerate,” as in John 6:60: “his doctrine was offensive to them. They hated it, and hence they perverted his meaning.” Clarke makes it pointed: his doctrine “comes too close to you; it searches your hearts, detects your hypocrisy… and as ye are determined not to leave your sins, so ye are purposed not to hear my doctrine.” Lightfoot illustrates from Isaiah 11:4 — “he shall smite the earth with the rod of his mouth” — for “they could not bear the smart of his rod” and so “would not understand the phraseology he used.”

Calvin, for the Reformed, reads it as a charge of obstinacy so great that they are “actuated and hurried away by diabolical rage.” Wesley draws the same conclusion and ties it to the chapter’s earlier principle: “such is your stubbornness and pride… not being desirous to do my will, ye cannot understand my doctrine” (John 7:17). The witnesses thus locate the failure not in the obscurity of Christ’s words but in the hostility of his hearers: the inability to understand is itself a moral inability, a refusal to bear a truth that condemns them. Their misunderstanding from v.33 onward is shown to be willful, the deafness of a heart that will not hear.

The witnesses draw the sobering lesson that unbelief is finally a matter of the will, not the intellect. Christ’s words were plain enough; what the Jews lacked was not light but the willingness to receive a light that exposed them. So their question, “Why do we not understand?”, is answered by a deeper diagnosis than they expected: they do not understand because they will not bear to — the surest proof that the fault lay not in the Teacher but in themselves.
44:
The pronoun carries the weight. “Ye” is emphatic, Ellicott insists — ye who have claimed both Abraham and God as father “are of the father, but that father is the devil” — and the possessive, he notes, is not expressed in the Greek at all. The father left unnamed at v.38 and v.41 is now named outright. Chrysostom marks the escalation: Christ, “having already cut off the Jews from relationship to Abraham, overthrows now this far greater claim, to call God their Father.” Ellicott also corrects the rendering of the second clause, where the verb is no mere auxiliary of the future but “expresses the determination of the will”: better, “ye desire to do, ye will to do” the lusts of that father.

The fathers at once guard the saying from misuse. Against “the heresy of the Manicheans, who hold a certain original nature of evil,” Augustine declares that “the Jews were children of the devil by imitation, not by birth” — “you are his children… because you have such lusts, not because you are born of him” — and Gill likewise denies that they are of the devil’s substance. Ellicott adds a caution against an old heretical construction of the first and last clauses, which made the Jews the offspring of the devil’s own father; revived, he says, “in some quarters in our own day,” it is “no less opposed to the context and the teaching of this Gospel than it is to the whole tenor of Biblical truth.”

On the first mark, murder, Ellicott reaches back to the Fall, citing Paul’s “by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin” (Romans 5:12). His formulation is compact: “the Fall was the murder of the human race,” and “the fratricide in the first family” was “a signal result” of it — “Cain was of that wicked one, and slew his brother.” The charge is raised here, he observes, precisely because the Jews “had been seeking to kill our Lord” (v.40). Augustine refers the murder to the first man, slain not by sword but by an evil word sown in him; Barnes and Robertson note the blunt compound behind the phrase (anthrōpoktonos, man-slayer), pointing to Adam’s ruin and Abel’s death (Genesis 3; 4:8; compare 1 John 3:12).

On the second mark, Ellicott again presses the tense: better “standeth not in the truth,” a present describing “his constant character,” not the fall, “which is here implied but not stated.” The devil “has no place in the sphere of the truth,” which is not the region of his action; and so there is none in the sphere of his thought either. Lightfoot offers a second sense: he did not persist in God’s revealed will concerning man. Charged to minister to man for his good (Hebrews 1:14), the devil, “envying the honour and happiness of man,” held the command in such contempt that he “chose rather to dethrone himself from his own glory and felicity, than he would bear Adam’s continuance in so noble a station” — an angel, Lightfoot adds, “was incapable of sinning either more or less than by pride or malice.”

The lie, finally, is his own property. Ellicott sets it against the work of Christ and of the Spirit, who “will not speak of Himself” but speaks what he heard from God, and renders the closing words “the father of the liar.” Westcott construes them differently, making the indefinite speaker rather than the devil the subject — a reading judged “a very doubtful expression.” Henry gathers the lusts as “spiritual wickedness… pride and envy, wrath and malice, enmity to good, and enticing others to evil”; and Calvin presses that it is by freely imitated works, not by any fate of nature, that hatred of the truth stamps a man as the liar’s child.
45:
The reversal named here is startling: truth itself becomes the ground of unbelief. The grammatical-historical commentators bring out the emphatic contrast. Ellicott reads the pronoun as “full of emphatic meaning — I, as contrary to him,” the devil, “because I tell you the truth, as contrary to the lie which is his characteristic.” He marks how arresting this is: “to speak the truth is commonly to command belief… the mind of man is so constituted that truth is the first object of its search,” yet “here was perfect truth presented to men, and they refused to accept it.” Robertson notes the proleptic, emphatic “I” and quotes Bernard: “truth is uncongenial to them,” pointing back to the verdict of John 3:19 — men loving darkness rather than light. Gill specifies the truth they reject as “the whole truth of the Gospel, and particularly the truth of his divine sonship.”

Calvin, for the Reformed, makes the verse confirm the preceding charge: “since they have no other reason for opposing, but because truth is hateful and intolerable to them, they show plainly that they are the children of Satan.” The point, the witnesses agree, is diagnostic. Ordinarily a hearer disbelieves because he doubts a claim is true; here the Jews disbelieve precisely because the claim is true, their hostility proof of a heart at enmity with truth itself. So Christ’s very faithfulness — telling them not flattering lies but the searching truth — becomes, in their hands, the occasion of their rejection, and thereby the clearest evidence of whose children they are. The verse thus stands as a mirror for every age: where truth provokes not belief but rage, the fault lies not in the truth but in the corrupt will that cannot bear it.

The witnesses press how the verse seals the indictment of the preceding ones. Having traced their unbelief to a father whose nature is falsehood (v.44), Christ now shows its symptom: they cannot abide the truth. A heart at home with the liar will find the truth-teller intolerable, and so the very perfection of Christ’s honesty becomes the stone over which they stumble. Their rejection, far from telling against his claim, is exactly what the gospel would predict of children of the father of lies.
46:
The challenge comes in two questions, and the first turns on how much “sin” is being claimed. The first question Robertson renders “which of you convicteth me of sin?” — the verb elenchō meaning to charge and prove (cf. John 16:8) — and takes “sin” “as in John 1:29” to mean “sin in general,” so that the unanswered question “involves sinlessness” (Hebrews 4:15) “without specifically saying so.” Ellicott agrees it is an appeal “to their knowledge of His sinless life” (v.29), “an appeal that spotless purity alone could make”; he pictures a pause after the challenge, during which “no one of all who had watched Him in Galilee and Judæa dared utter a syllable” — “their silence is the seal” of his innocence. But Barnes and Clarke press a narrower sense: since “sin” here “stands opposed to truth” in the same verse, it should be rendered “error, falsehood, or imposture” — “which of you can prove that I am an impostor?” On this reading the argument is that a doctrine may be rejected only if its teacher is shown to be a deceiver, and they cannot show it.

Calvin, for the Reformed, hears “perfect confidence”: knowing “they could not justly bring any reproach against him, he glories over his enemies, as having obtained a victory” — not that he was free from their slanders, but that “no crime dwells in him.” Wesley draws the practical point: “is not my life as unreprovable as my doctrine? Does not my whole behaviour confirm the truth of what I teach?” The witnesses thus find in the verse both a unique self-witness and an unanswerable argument: the sinless (or, on the other reading, the guileless) Teacher binds his hearers to believe, since they can convict him of neither sin nor fraud, and their unbelief is therefore, as Robertson says, sheer irrationality “based on prejudice and predilection.”

The witnesses also note the boldness of so public a challenge. No mere man could stand before lifelong enemies, who had watched his every step, and dare them to name a single sin; yet Jesus does, and the silence that answers is itself a testimony. Whether the word means moral fault or fraud, the effect is the same: they can convict him of neither, and so their refusal to believe is left without excuse, resting, as Robertson says, on nothing but prejudice.
47:
Ellicott reads the verse as Christ answering his own question of v.46, and giving more fully the reason already offered at v.43. The symmetry with v.44 is exact: having asserted that they were of the father the devil and therefore lived to do the devil’s lusts, he now states the converse: whoever is of God does God’s will and hears his words. The words meant are no abstraction — Ellicott identifies them as those “which He has been speaking unto them” at v.26.

Barnes defines the hearing as attending to the doctrines and commandments of God “as a child who loves his parent will regard and obey” — an evidence of true piety, since readiness to receive all that God teaches and to obey all he enjoins is, in his phrase, “an undoubted proof that we are his friends” (John 14:21; 1 John 2:4; 1 John 3:24). Wesley catches the manner of it in three words: such a man hears “with joy and reverence.” Robertson, citing Dods, states the inference without softening — “their not listening proved that they were not of God” — and refers the construction to the same use of the preposition at John 3:31.

Gill presses the other half — what it is to belong to God — and answers by the new birth. Such a man is born “not of blood, by carnal descent from any person, or of the carnal will, or by the power of freewill, or of the will of the best man in the world; but of God,” according to his abundant mercy and “by the power of his grace,” and so has God for his Father.

Clarke dissents, and the dissent changes the verse. He takes the opening phrase to designate “probably himself: he who came from God, or was born of God,” whose hearing of God’s words consists in having “the constant inspiration of his Spirit,” so that he “speaks nothing but truth, and cannot possibly err.” On that reading the first clause is not a test of discipleship at all but a claim about the speaker, and the rebuke that follows rests on their refusal of a messenger who cannot be mistaken.

Calvin tracks the rising temper of the exchange. Entitled to take for granted that he is “the ambassador of the heavenly Father,” and having shown that they could allege nothing he had not taught as from the mouth of God, Christ “kindles into greater indignation against them; for their impiety was no longer concealed.” He therefore “concludes that they have nothing in common with God, for they do not hear the words of God,” and — this is Calvin’s point — “without saying any thing about himself, he charges them with being at war with God.” From it Calvin draws a diagnostic that cuts both ways: there is “not a more evident sign of a reprobate mind, than when one cannot endure the doctrine of Christ,” whereas to embrace that doctrine cheerfully is “a visible seal of our election.” He who has the word “enjoys God himself; but he who rejects it excludes himself from righteousness and life.” Ellicott’s closing inventory shows how little religious standing weighs against that: Rabbis and priests, teachers of the Law, judges of truth, offerers of sacrifice, keepers of feasts, worshippers in synagogue and Temple — “they were all this; but they were not ‘of God.’”
48:
Argument having failed, malice takes its place. The Eastern Chrysostom observes that “a shameless and a forward thing is wickedness, and when it ought to hide itself, then is it the fiercer”: when they should have been “pricked” and won by “the boldness and conclusiveness of the words,” they instead “insult Him.” The grammatical-historical commentators explain the two slurs. “Samaritan,” Barnes and Clarke note, was a term of contempt equivalent to “heretic” or “schismatic,” one “unworthy of any credit” (cf. John 4:9); Robertson says they knew he was no Samaritan but charged it because “he had acted like a Samaritan in challenging their peculiar spiritual privileges.” The charge of “hast a devil” — “art possessed… and art, in consequence, deranged” (Clarke) — was, Robertson notes, “an old one” (Matthew 12:24) and would be repeated (John 10:20). Lightfoot exposes the insincerity: would they really suffer a Samaritan to stand “in the Treasury” (v.20)? — proof the slur was “spoken in rancour and mere malice,” they “perfectly knowing that he was no Samaritan.”

The Latin Augustine turns the scene to instruction: “from power we learn patience.” Christ, “the Just One” and “the Creator,” bore “Thou hast a devil” without retaliation; “let him first imitate His patience” who would attain his power. Henry, for the Puritans, marks that those who now fall “to downright railing” were “the men of consequence,” the scribes and Pharisees, who, “convicted of an obstinate infidelity, scornfully turned off the conviction” with abuse. Calvin, for the Reformed, sees them “stupefied by Satan,” so desperate that, “fully convicted, still they are enraged.” The witnesses thus read the railing as the confession of a beaten cause: unable to answer the truth or convict its Teacher of sin, they can only revile him — and in reviling the sinless One as devil-possessed, they betray once more whose children they are.

There is irony in it: calling the sinless One a demoniac, the Jews unwittingly repeat the sin Christ had just exposed. Unable to convict him of any fault (v.46) or to answer his reasoning, they resort to the weapon of the father of lies — slander. Their railing is thus not a refutation but a confession; the very abuse they hurl is the mark of the paternity he has charged upon them, and it leaves his argument wholly untouched.
49:
The reply answers one charge and lets the other lie. Gill observes that Christ “takes no notice of the first” — the name “Samaritan” — because it was “so notorious” that he was not one; it was in any case a term of abuse rather than an accusation. Ellicott makes the silence more pointed still: the words Christ spoke soon after “taught that a Samaritan may be more truly the child of God than priest or Levite is.” What he does deny is the graver thing, that he was possessed by an evil power from the unseen world. Robertson and Ellicott both note the restraint of the answer, which meets calumny with a bare statement of fact rather than counter-railing. Ellicott adds that one of the disciples, “probably present on this day,” afterwards wrote of this very example — of him “who, when He was reviled, reviled not again; when He suffered He threatened not; but committed Himself to Him that judgeth righteously” (1 Peter 2:23).

The positive half of the reply Ellicott takes as the real refutation. “There is a connection between all His works and words and the unseen world,” but it is “the union of Father and Son,” and his life “had been the constant honouring of the Father, whose will it was His meat to do” (John 4:31). Their words and works were as constantly dishonouring him — “and this last calumny is an instance of it.” The contrast carries further than they intended, for the dishonour “was not of Him only; but also of the Father whom He honoured, and whom they claimed as their God.”

Here the witnesses divide. Augustine, as Calvin reports him, read the first charge allegorically and held that Christ “did not refuse to be called” a Samaritan, since the name suited him as a true guardian of his flock. Calvin judges otherwise. The two reproaches, he argues, “had the same object,” so that “by refuting the one, he refutes the other”; and of the two it was the charge of possession, not the national slur, that insulted him the more grievously. On Calvin’s reading Christ “satisfies himself with a simple refutation, which he draws from what is contrary,” asserting that he labours to promote his Father’s honour — “for he who duly and sincerely honors him must be guided by the Spirit of God, and must be a faithful servant of God.”

Calvin then presses the claim higher. Rather than a complaint that he is denied the honour due him, he takes Christ to be joining the Father’s glory to his own, and puts the sense in Christ’s mouth: “I claim nothing for myself which does not tend to the glory of God; for his majesty shines in me, his power and authority dwells in me; and therefore, when you treat me so disdainfully, you pour contempt on God himself.” That is why the next clause can announce that God will avenge the insult — Christ cared about the honour shown him not “from any personal feelings of a carnal nature” but only “so far as the honour or contempt of God is concerned.” Calvin turns it finally to the reader: let any man sincerely desirous of God’s glory be assured of God’s commendation, since “those who honor me, I will render honorable” (1 Samuel 2:30); and if men “not only despise, but even load him with reproaches, let him calmly wait till the day of the Lord come.”
50:
Christ commits his vindication to another, and the commentators begin with his self-denial. “In all his teaching this was true,” Barnes says: “he did not seek to exalt or to vindicate himself. He was willing to lie under reproach and to be despised,” and so “regarded little” their taunts and accusations. Ellicott observes that the words “repeat what He had taught them before” (John 5:41; John 7:18), and draws the consequence exactly: “for Him whose whole life was one of self-denial, their dishonour finds nothing which it can wound.” Robertson sets the claim against the men who made it, who “did not seek the glory of God” (John 5:44).

On the second clause the witnesses agree that the one who seeks is the Father, who “seeketh for the honour of the Son, and judgeth between Him and those who dishonour Him” (Ellicott; compare John 5:45). Barnes puts it in the first person: “God will take care of my reputation. He seeks my welfare and honour, and I may commit my cause into his hands without attempting my own vindication.” Robertson adds a careful balance — the Father “judges between you and me, though the Son is the Judge of mankind” (John 5:22) — and quotes Bernard’s verdict that “it is only the glory that comes from God that is worth having.” Gill grounds the serenity in Christ’s certainty that “Wisdom was justified of her children,” so that “he committed himself to God that judgeth righteously, who would take care of his glory, and vindicate him.” Clarke and Wesley hear in the word “judgeth” a quiet warning as well: the Father who seeks the Son’s honour will pass sentence accordingly on their obstinacy.

From this passage Barnes draws three lessons, and they are the most practical thing said on the verse. First, that “where men have no sound arguments, they attempt to overwhelm their adversaries by calling odious and reproachful names”; accusations of heresy and schism, and reproachful terms generally, are “commonly proof” not only of unchristian feeling but “that they have no sound reasons to support their cause.” Second, that while it is right to vindicate oneself against such charges, “it should not be done by rendering railing for railing” — rather, “in meekness we should instruct those that oppose themselves, if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth” (2 Timothy 2:25). Third, that lying under reproach is not “necessarily dishonourable.” Where a man has a good conscience, has examined the matter for himself, and is conscious of seeking God’s glory, he “should be willing, as Jesus was, to bear reproach, believing that God will in due time avenge us, and bring forth our righteousness as the light, and our judgment as the noon-day” (Psalm 37:6).
51:
The promise is introduced with the formula of solemn asseveration, and the commentators define both its condition and its gift with care. The grammatical-historical commentators define both the condition and the gift. To “keep my word” (Robertson notes the better reading, a third-class condition) is, Barnes says, to “believe on me and obey my commandments” — the phrase recurring through John (John 14:23; 1 John 2:5) and equivalent to keeping his commands. “Never see death” is a Hebraism (Psalm 89:48) for never dying, and means here, all agree, spiritual and eternal death: “he shall obtain eternal life” (Barnes; cf. John 5:24; John 11:25). Ellicott makes John 5:24 the key — “he that heareth my word… passeth from death unto life” — the believer possessing now “the true spiritual life which cannot see death.” Clarke draws the contrast with Moses, who “promised a long life” to the law-keeper, whereas Christ promises that the keeper of his word “shall never come under the power of the death of the soul, but shall live eternally.”

Henry, for the Puritans, calls it “the doctrine of the immortality of believers,” and unfolds “the character of a believer” as one who keeps Christ’s word — receiving it, holding it “in mind and memory… in love and affection.” Calvin, for the Reformed, reads the verse as Christ’s deliberate turn from threatening to comfort: knowing “some persons in that multitude were curable,” he “intended to terrify the wicked… but in such a manner as to leave ground of consolation for the good,” so that “the faithful teacher ought not to be wholly employed in reproving the wicked, but ought also to impart the doctrine of salvation to the children of God.” Wesley adds that we keep his word “by believing his promises… by obeying his command,” and that the promise of deathlessness itself “proves that he was no Samaritan, for the Samaritans were Sadducees.” The witnesses thus find in this verse the gracious counterpart to the chapter’s severity — the offer of life that never dies to all who keep the word of Christ.
52:
A fresh blasphemy follows, and beneath it lies a stubborn literalism. The grammatical-historical commentators explain that, taking Christ’s words “in a merely physical sense” (Ellicott), they find them flatly “contradicted by the fact that death came to the great Patriarch and the prophets,” and conclude that “no one, except a man under the influence of a demon, would make an assertion so opposed to the almost unbroken experience of mankind.” Robertson marks the perfect tense “now we know” (egnōkamen), “a state of completion” — “now since such talk we have come to certain knowledge that thou hast a demon” — and notes they subtly shift his “see death” to “taste of death.” Origen observes that they reckoned Christ to speak “by the influence of the devil… because they did not know the power of God.”

The fathers supply the deeper irony. Gregory remarks that “as it is necessary that the good should grow better by contumely, so are the reprobate made worse by kindness” — the very promise of life provoking their blasphemy. Theophylact and Augustine, looking ahead to v.55, read “I keep his saying” of the Son’s unchanging unity with the Father. Calvin, for the Reformed, exposes their error precisely: they “apply the spiritual doctrine of Christ to the body.” In the sense Christ intends, no believer dies at all. Calvin rests this on the new birth (1 Peter 1:23): believers live even when they die, since, “united to Christ their Head, they cannot be extinguished by death,” and death is to them a passage into the heavenly kingdom. The witnesses thus find the Jews condemned out of their own literalism: dragging a promise of eternal life down to the level of the body, they call the Author of life a demoniac, and so prove again how the same word that saves the believing hardens the reprobate.

The witnesses observe that the Jews, in their confidence, suppose themselves to have caught Christ in an absurdity, when in truth they have only displayed their own deafness to spiritual things. Abraham and the prophets did die in the body, but they live unto God; and the very promise the Jews deride is the hope in which the fathers themselves rested. Their triumphant ‘now we know’ is thus the surest proof of how little they know — measuring the words of the Lord of life by the bare experience of the grave.
53:
The retort carries both the old pride of descent and a half-glimpsed suspicion of blasphemy. The grammatical-historical commentators note the question echoes the Samaritan woman’s about Jacob (John 4:12), with Abraham substituted; Robertson observes the form expects the answer “no” — “surely thou art not greater than our father Abraham” — and that “they do not see that Jesus uses death in a different sense.” Barnes catches the scorn: that “a Nazarene, a Samaritan, and a devil” should claim to keep his followers from dying was a question “implying… contempt and scorn.” Yet the sharper edge is in “whom makest thou thyself?” — a predicate accusative by which, Robertson notes, “they suspect that Jesus is guilty of blasphemy as they charged in John 5:18,” a charge they will later make explicit (John 10:33; John 19:7). Ellicott frames their reasoning: “if Abraham… himself died, and if the prophets… themselves died, what kind of person dost Thou assert Thyself to be that Thy word shall deliver men from death?”

Calvin, for the Reformed, names the offence beneath the question: they “endeavour to obscure the glory of Christ by the splendour of Abraham and of the saints.” But “as all the stars are thrown into the shade by the brightness of the sun, so all the glory… in all the saints must fade away before the incomparable brightness of Christ”; to contrast “the servants with the Lord” is to “act unjustly and absurdly,” and to abuse the very name of the fathers “in opposition to Christ.” The witnesses thus find the Jews stumbling, without knowing it, over the true answer: he is indeed greater than Abraham and the prophets, the Lord whose word gives the life that even the patriarchs awaited — a greatness the next verses will declare in the most startling terms.

The question is more apt than its askers knew. ‘Whom makest thou thyself?’ is asked in scorn, yet it touches the very point at issue: not whom Christ pretends to be, but who he truly is. He makes himself nothing, as the next verse will say; it is the Father who makes him great. And the answer they could not bear is precisely the one the chapter is moving toward — that he is greater than Abraham because, before Abraham was, he is.
54:
Christ refers his glory once more to the Father, and in doing so exposes the emptiness of the Jews’ claim on God. The grammatical-historical commentators note the principle, already stated at John 5:31: self-sought honour “is of no value” (Barnes), “empty and vain” (Gill). His true honour comes from another — “it is my Father that honoureth me” — so that, in answering “whom makest thou thyself?”, Christ replies that he makes himself nothing, but is made glorious by the Father (cf. John 17:1). The sting lies in the closing clause: the Father who honours him is the very God “of whom ye say, that he is your God” — a God they claim but, as the next verse will say, do not know. Clarke notes the textual variation between “your God” and “our God,” but the point holds either way.

Henry, for the Puritans, and Calvin, for the Reformed, press the irony. The Jews boast of God as theirs while dishonouring the Son he honours; their religion is loud in profession and empty in reality. Calvin observes that Christ “does not simply claim glory for himself, but ascribes it wholly to the Father,” and thereby convicts them of a hollow piety — claiming God with their lips while rejecting the One whom God exalts. The witnesses thus find in the verse a double movement: Christ’s perfect humility, refusing all self-glory and resting in the Father’s honour; and the unmasking of his accusers, whose proud claim “he is your God” is about to be answered with the charge that they have never truly known him. The boast of God on their lips becomes the measure of their condemnation.

The reply answers their taunt exactly. They had asked whom he made himself; he replies that he makes himself nothing, claiming no honour but what the Father gives. So the charge of self-exaltation falls to the ground, and rebounds upon them: it is they who exalt themselves in claiming a God they do not know, while the One they accuse seeks only the Father’s glory. The contrast between true and false honour is laid bare, and with it the emptiness of a religion that boasts in God yet rejects his Son.
55:
The contrast between Christ and his accusers reaches its sharpest point here. The grammatical-historical commentators draw out the two halves. On the Jews’ side, their boast “he is your God” (v.54) is hollow, for “ye have not known him”; their claim to God is contradicted by their rejection of the Son whom God sent, so that they are revealed as ignorant of the very God they profess. On Christ’s side stands the calm, unqualified “but I know him” — a knowledge, Robertson and Ellicott note, that is immediate and perfect, the knowledge of the Son who is from the Father. The middle clause presses the point with startling force: were Christ to deny that knowledge, “I shall be a liar like unto you” — that is, to disclaim his unique knowledge of the Father, to dissemble out of false modesty, would make him as false as they. Truth itself compels him to assert what they count blasphemy.

Gill marks that Christ adds the proof of his knowledge — “and keep his saying” — for to know the Father and to keep his word are inseparable; the Son’s obedience attests his knowledge. The witnesses thus find the verse setting an unbridgeable distance between the two parties: the accusers, loud in their claim on God yet strangers to him; and the accused, who knows the Father with a knowledge so certain that to deny it would be the one lie he could not tell. Far from the demoniac boaster they have called him, Christ stands as the truthful witness whose very honesty requires him to confess the intimacy with God that his hearers lack — and which the following verses will trace back before Abraham himself.

The witnesses press the boldness of the middle clause. Christ will not, even to soften their fury, pretend to less than he is; to disown his knowledge of the Father would be the one falsehood incompatible with his nature as the Truth. So the same honesty that the Jews counted blasphemy is in fact the proof of his integrity — he speaks the unwelcome truth of his unique knowledge of God precisely because he cannot lie. Here, as throughout the chapter, truthfulness itself divides him utterly from the children of the father of lies.
56:
Christ answers the challenge of “art thou greater than Abraham?” (v.53) — turning the patriarch they claimed into a witness against them. The grammatical-historical commentators dwell on the word “rejoiced” (ēgalliasato): it “includes the notion of desire as well as rejoicing” (Barnes), and Clarke pictures the soul of Abraham leaping “forward in earnest hope and strong expectation,” like one who runs to meet a long-awaited friend. Robertson links it to Hebrews 11:13, the fathers “saluting the promises from afar.” On how Abraham “saw” the day, the commentators offer several modes: by faith in the promise that in his seed all nations should be blessed (Genesis 22:18; Ellicott, Wesley), in types and theophanies such as the appearance at Mamre (Genesis 18:1; Wesley), and perhaps in the vision of Genesis 15 (Robertson notes a Jewish tradition that Abraham then saw his descendants’ whole history). Ellicott draws the contrast sharply: Abraham “realised the fulness of the promises… exulting” to see the Messiah from afar, while these, his supposed children, reject the Messiah “actually among them.”

Calvin, for the Reformed, makes the contrast the heart of the verse: Abraham “had no other object during his whole life than to see my kingdom flourish; he longed for me when I was absent, you despise me when I am present.” And what is true of Abraham “applies to all the saints,” though “with greater weight in the person of Abraham, because he is the father of the whole Church”: “whoever desires to be reckoned in the number of the godly, let him rejoice… in the presence of Christ, for which Abraham ardently longed.” Cyril of Jerusalem turns it to the Son’s eternity, citing Micah 5:2 — his “goings forth are from… the days of eternity.” The witnesses thus find the verse both honouring Abraham’s forward-looking faith and condemning the Jews: the father they boast of welcomed the very Christ they would stone.

The witnesses observe how the verse quietly establishes Christ’s superiority to Abraham, which the Jews had challenged. Abraham is great, but his greatness lay in longing for and welcoming the day of Christ; the patriarch was the servant who awaited his Lord. To set Abraham above Christ, then, is to mistake the worshipper for the One worshipped — and the chapter is about to show, in the plainest words, just how far above Abraham the Son in truth stands.
57:
The objection is carnally literal, and it quietly perverts what Christ had said. Gregory observes that “the carnal minds of the Jews are intent on the flesh only; they think only of His age in the flesh,” reckoning the centuries since Abraham died. The grammatical-historical commentators add that they have twisted his claim: Christ said Abraham saw his day, but they retort, “hast thou seen Abraham?” (Barnes). On the round number “fifty,” the commentators differ: Jesus was about thirty-three (Theophylact, Gill), so some ask why not “forty.” Robertson calls fifty “the crisis of completed manhood” (Numbers 4:3) and “a round number”; Lightfoot ties it to the age of the Levites’ superannuation (Numbers 4); Gill suggests his face, “a man of sorrows,” made him look older. Ellicott defends the reading “fifty” against the ancient substitution of “forty,” noting that some Elders who “conferred with John” (reported by Irenaeus) even held Jesus to have been between forty and fifty. Robertson records the textual variant by which some manuscripts read “hath Abraham seen thee?”

Calvin, for the Reformed, sees them trying “to refute Christ’s saying by showing that he had asserted what was impossible.” They allow him to be “somewhat older” than he was, “that they may not appear too rigid,” as if to say, “Thou certainly wilt not make thyself so old, though thou wert to boast.” He dismisses the notion of Papias that Christ lived more than forty years. The witnesses thus find the Jews, fixed on the flesh, walking straight into the answer they cannot conceive: their scornful arithmetic — fifty years against two thousand — measures only the man they see, and leaves them wholly unprepared for the claim of eternal being that Christ is about to make. Their question about age is about to be answered by a word that lifts him clean out of time.

A deeper irony lies underneath. Confident that they have exposed an impossibility, the Jews have in fact set the stage for the most stupendous claim of the Gospel. They reckon by years and decades; Christ is about to answer in the language of eternity. Their very objection — measuring him against the centuries since Abraham — invites the reply that he is before Abraham altogether, the timeless ‘I am’ whom no reckoning of years can contain.
58:
The answer is given under the formula of solemn asseveration, and the commentators ground its force in the grammar. Robertson is emphatic that the contrast between “before Abraham came into existence” (prin Abraham genesthai) and the timeless “I am” (egō eimi) is “complete” — “undoubtedly here Jesus claims eternal existence with the absolute phrase used of God.” Ellicott draws the same line: “Abraham, like all men, came into being. There was a time when he was not. But there was never a time when the Son of God was not… He is the I AM, present equally in the human ‘was,’ and ‘is,’ and ‘is to come’” (compare John 1:1). Barnes observes that the present tense, used of God, “denotes continued existence without respect to time,” as in “from everlasting to everlasting thou art God” (Psalm 90:2). Lightfoot points out that the Jews had perverted the question — Christ had spoken of Abraham seeing his day, they of his seeing Abraham — and that he answers on a wholly higher plane.

Clarke gives the verse at length in a translation of Calmet’s note, which puts the claim as a distinction of natures. “I am from all eternity. I have existed before all ages. You consider in me only the person who speaks to you, and who has appeared to you within a particular time. But besides this human nature, which ye think ye know, there is in me a Divine and eternal nature. Both, united, subsist together in my person.” The patriarch, on this reading, knew how to tell the two apart: “he adored me as his God; and desired me as his Savior. He has seen me in my eternity, and he predicted my coming into the world.”

Clarke sets beside it a note of Bishop Pearce’s that closes off a weaker reading. The words, Pearce argues, relate “to his existence antecedent to Abraham’s days, and not to his having been the Christ appointed and foretold before that time.” His reason is one of relevance: had Jesus meant only that he was foreordained, “the answer I apprehend would not have been a pertinent one.” A man may be foreordained and predicted and still not yet exist; but then he could neither have seen Abraham, nor Abraham have seen him, which is precisely what the preceding exchange had been about. Only actual pre-existence answers what was asked.

The wording inevitably recalls the divine Name, “I AM THAT I AM” (Exodus 3:14), the self-designation that has sounded through the chapter already (vv.24, 28). Calvin and Wesley alike take the sentence as the plainest assertion of Christ’s eternal Godhead, Wesley glossing it simply “even from everlasting to everlasting.” To the scornful question how a man not yet fifty could have seen Abraham, the reply is not that he is older than Abraham, but that he is before and above all reckoning of time.
59:
The stones are themselves the proof that the claim had been understood exactly. The grammatical-historical commentators note that they reached for stones because they heard in “Before Abraham was, I am” the blasphemy of a man making himself God (the penalty for which was stoning, Leviticus 24:16); Gill and Lightfoot add that the temple, then still under construction, lay ready with building-stones to hand. That their fury was kindled by the claim of deity, the commentators agree, confirms the sense of v.58 — they took it as no less than a claim to be God. The withdrawal, Robertson and Ellicott note, is told simply: “Jesus hid himself” (ekrybē) and passed out through their midst, his hour not yet come (cf. John 7:30).

The Latin fathers find in the scene both doctrine and mystery. Augustine fastens on the grammar he has been pressing: Christ “did not say, before Abraham was, but, before Abraham was made,” for Abraham is “a creature,” while of the Word it stands written “in the beginning WAS the Word”; nor does he say “I was made,” because he simply is. Gregory adds that “their unbelieving minds were unable to support these indications of eternity, and, not understanding Him, sought to destroy Him.” Augustine reads even the withdrawal tenderly: having “done all that He could do as a teacher,” and meeting only stones, “He leaves them,” yet “did not hide Himself” as one afraid, but as one whose time was not yet. The witnesses thus close the chapter on its sharpest contrast: the eternal “I am” offering life and light, and the children of the father of murder answering with stones — and the One they cannot seize passing untouched through their midst, master still of the hour of his death.

The witnesses draw the chapter’s closing lesson from the violence and the escape together. That the Jews answered a claim of grace and life with stones lays bare the murderous spirit Christ had charged upon them (v.44); and that he passed unharmed through their midst shows that, even in the face of death, he remained sovereign over his own hour. The Light of the world, rejected and assailed, withdraws — not defeated, but in command — leaving his hearers to the darkness they have chosen.
